t: A traditional kitchen scale balances. On the left pan there is a mystery weight and a three gram weight. On the right pan there is a ten gram weight. How heavy is the mystery weight, in grams? The picture shows: A kitchen scale that balances. Left pan: a mystery weight (?) and a three gram weight. Right pan: a ten gram weight.
Last time: work out three plus four times two.
Work out minus two plus five.
Work out two times (three plus four).

Key idea: we leave out the times sign: three n means three times n, and ab means eigh times b. Write the number first: three n, not n3. This is a convention, an agreed habit, so that everyone reads algebra the same way. And eigh times a is written eigh squared. The letter is a placeholder for a number, so everything you know about numbers still works.
If n equals four, what is n plus seven? The picture shows: A function machine. The input is four. The machine adds seven. The output is unknown.
If n equals five, what is three n?
If n equals ten, what is the fraction n over two,?
Which expression means five less than n?
Which expression means double n, then add three?
A tube of blue paint costs £b. Zara buys three tubes and a two pounds brush. Write an expression for the total cost in pounds. (Type it like three b plus two.)

Key idea: write the letter's value in brackets when you substitute, especially for negatives: for x squared with x equals minus three, write (minus three) squared equals nine. Without brackets you might compute minus three squared equals minus nine, which is not the same.
Work out two x plus three when x equals four. The picture shows: A function machine. The input x is four. The machine multiplies by two, then adds three. The output is unknown.
Work out five eigh minus two when eigh equals three. The picture shows: A function machine. The input a is three. The machine multiplies by five, then subtracts two. The output is unknown.
Work out x squared when x equals minus three. The picture shows: A function machine. The input x is minus three. The machine squares it, which means multiplying it by itself. The output is unknown.
Work out three(y plus two) when y equals one.
Work out eigh plus b when eigh equals two and b equals minus five.
Work out two x squared when x equals three.
A tube of blue paint costs £b. Zara buys three tubes and a two pounds brush, so the cost is three b plus two pounds. Work out the cost when b equals four.
A playlist has a three-minute intro and then four songs of s minutes each. It lasts four s plus three minutes. Work out how long it lasts when s equals three point five.

Key idea: three eigh plus two eigh equals five a is like three apples plus two apples equals five apples. It works because a is the same number in both terms: three eigh plus two eigh equals (three plus two)a. A letter is a number, not an object. But three apples plus two bananas stays as three apples plus two bananas, and three eigh plus two b stays as it is, because a and b can be different numbers. Each term keeps the sign in front of it, so in five x plus two minus x plus four the x terms are five x and minus x (which is minus one x).
Simplify three eigh plus two eigh. The picture shows: Three pink tiles each labelled a, standing for three eigh, next to two blue tiles each labelled a, standing for two eigh.
Simplify seven x minus three x.
Simplify four eigh plus three b plus two eigh. (Type it like five p plus two q.)
Simplify five x plus two minus x plus four. (Type it like three k-seven.)
Write eigh times a as simply as possible. (Type it like m squared.)
Write three times eigh times b as simply as possible. (Type it like four rs.)

Tiles are laid in a row: three pink tiles and two blue tiles, each a cm long, and four gold tiles, each one centimetre long. Write the total length in cm in its simplest form. (Type it like seven b plus two.) The picture shows: A row of tiles. Three pink tiles and two blue tiles are each a centimetres long. Four small gold tiles are each one centimetre long.

Key idea: the number outside multiplies both terms. three(x plus four) equals three x plus twelve, not three x plus four. If there is a minus inside, keep the sign: two(eigh minus five) equals two eigh minus ten, because two times (minus five) equals minus ten.

A sketchbook cover is three centimetres tall and (x plus four) cm wide. Expand three(x plus four) to write its area. (Type it like three x plus twelve.) The picture shows: A rectangle of height three and width x plus four, cut into a piece of width x and a piece of width four. The area of each piece is unknown.
The sketchbook cover's area is three(x plus four) equals three x plus twelve centimetres squared. Work out the area when x equals five, in cm squared.
Expand two(eigh minus five). (Type it like four metres-six.)

Expand five(two y plus one). (Type it like three k plus eight.) The picture shows: A rectangle of height five and width two y plus one, cut into a piece of width two y and a piece of width one. The area of each piece is unknown.
Expand four(m plus three) and then work out its value when m equals two.

Key idea: putting the right value for the unknown is what makes both sides of the equals the same. That value is the solution. For x plus three equals ten the right value is x equals seven, because seven plus three equals ten and the scale balances.
x plus three equals ten. What value of x makes both sides equal?
x plus seven equals twelve. Does x equals five make the scale balance? The picture shows: A kitchen scale. Left pan: a weight x and a seven gram weight. Right pan: a twelve gram weight.
two x equals fourteen. What value of x makes both sides equal?
x minus four equals nine. What value of x makes both sides equal?
You put five grams more in the left pan. What keeps the scale balanced?

Key idea: substituting and solving are two directions of the same relationship. In the same way, expanding and factorising are a pair. Both are the one statement three(x plus four) equals three x plus twelve, read in opposite directions.

two x plus three equals eleven. Find the value of x that makes both sides equal. The picture shows: A kitchen scale. Left pan: two equal weights x and a three gram weight. Right pan: an eleven gram weight.
three x plus twelve equals three(?). Fill in the bracket. (Type it like n plus six.)
six x plus nine equals three(?). Fill in the bracket. (Type it like three n plus five.)
A rule: multiply n by three, then add one. When n equals one, two, three the answers are four, seven, ten. What is the answer when n equals ten?

A different rule is three n plus two. When the answer is seventeen, what was n? The picture shows: An inverse function machine, run backwards from the answer. The start is seventeen. The first step subtracts two. The second step divides by three. The finish is the unknown n.
Pat says: three eigh plus two b equals five ab. What went wrong?
Quin says: two(x plus three) equals two x plus three. What went wrong?
Rae says: When x equals four, three x equals thirty-four. What went wrong?
Work out five x minus x squared when x equals two.
Simplify eight x minus three x plus two x. (Type it like four k.)
Expand four(x minus two). (Type it like three metres-five.)
Work out three n plus ten when n equals minus two. The picture shows: A function machine. The input n is minus two. The machine multiplies by three, then adds ten. The output is unknown.
Which of these is NOT a like term with three eigh: five eigh, eigh squared or seven eigh?
Work out the value of two x squared minus three x when x equals minus two.
Simplify four x plus three minus x plus five. (Type it like five p-two.)
Expand and simplify two(x plus three) plus three(x minus one). (Type it like five x plus three.)
Work out x squared plus three x when x equals minus two.
Simplify two(three x plus one) minus four x. (Type it like six k-one.)

Expand (x plus one)(x plus four). (Type it like x squared plus three x plus two.) The picture shows: A grid with x and four across the top and x and one down the side. The four cell areas are unknown.

Expand (x plus five)(x plus two). (Type it like x squared plus six x plus eight.) The picture shows: A grid with x and two across the top and x and five down the side. The four cell areas are unknown.
Expand (x plus three)(x minus one). (Type it like x squared-x-six.)

A plumber works out a quote with C equals forty-five plus thirty-eight h, where C is the cost in pounds, forty-five is the call-out fee (a fixed charge for coming to the job) and h is the number of hours. Find C when h equals three point five. Give your answer in pounds.

A quote is C equals sixty plus forty-two h plus m, where h is the hours of labour and m is the cost of parts in pounds. Find C when h equals two point five and m equals eighty-six point four zero. Type it like forty-two point seven five.

The number of zero point five metre square tiles needed for a floor is n equals four lw, where l is the length and w is the width of the floor, both in metres. Find n when l equals three point five and w equals two point five. The picture shows: A rectangle made of a grid of square tiles, seven tiles along the length and five tiles across the width. The length is labelled three point five metres and the width is labelled two point five metres. Each tile is zero point five metres by zero point five metres.

A quote with VAT is C equals one point two(forty-five plus thirty-eight h plus m), where h is the hours of labour and m is the cost of parts in pounds. Find C when h equals two and m equals fifty-four point five zero. Type it like forty-two point seven five.
The volume of water in a round pipe is V equals three point one four r squared h, where r is the radius and h is the length, both in cm. Find V when r equals two and h equals ten, in cm cubed.

How to type algebraic fractions on this page: write the numerator, a slash, then the denominator. Put brackets round the numerator or the denominator if it has more than one term. For example (x plus one)/(x-two), three/x or (two x plus three)/six. Type x squared as x squared. Where there are two answers, type them like two,3.
Write the fraction six over nine, in its simplest form. Type it like three over four.
Work out the fraction one over three, plus the fraction one over four,. Type it like five over eight.
Factorise x squared plus five x plus six. Type it like (x plus one)(x plus four).
Factorise x squared minus nine. Type it like (x plus one)(x-one).

Key idea: you can only cancel a factor (something multiplied), never a term (something added). In the fraction x plus five over x, the x in the numerator is added to five, so it cannot be cancelled. In the fraction five x over x, the x is multiplied, so it can.
Simplify the fraction six x over nine,.
Simplify the fraction twelve x squared over eight x,.
Simplify the fraction three x squared over six x cubed,.
Which of these fractions can be simplified by cancelling?

A rectangular panel has an area of twelve x squared cm squared and a width of four x cm. Write its length as a simplified expression, in cm. The picture shows: A rectangle. Its area is twelve x squared square centimetres and its width is four x centimetres. The length is marked with a question mark.

Key idea: factorise, then cancel whole brackets. The tools you already have: take out a common factor, quadratics like x squared plus five x plus six equals (x plus two)(x plus three), and the Difference of two squares: x squared minus nine equals (x plus three)(x minus three).
Simplify the fraction three x plus six over three,.
Simplify the fraction five x plus ten over x plus two,.
Simplify the fraction x squared plus four x over x,.
Simplify the fraction x squared minus twenty-five over x plus five,.
Simplify the fraction x squared plus seven x plus ten over x plus two,.
Simplify the fraction x squared minus nine over x squared plus x minus six,.
Which is the fraction x squared plus six x plus eight over x squared plus two x, in its simplest form?
Simplify the fraction x squared minus four over two x minus four,.

A rectangular lawn has an area of (x squared plus five x plus six) m squared and a width of (x plus two) m. Find its length, as an expression in x, in m. The picture shows: A rectangle. The area is x squared plus five x plus six square metres. The width is x plus two metres. The length is marked with a question mark.
Key idea: multiply numerators, multiply denominators, and cancel matching factors. To divide, flip the second fraction first. If a bracket is in the numerator and the denominator, it cancels.
Work out the fraction x over five, times the fraction ten over x squared,.
Work out the fraction x plus two over three, times the fraction six over x plus two,.
Work out the fraction x over four, divided by the fraction x over eight,.
Work out the fraction x squared over six, divided by the fraction x over three,.
Work out the fraction x plus three over x minus one, times the fraction x minus one over two,.
Simplify fully the fraction x squared plus three x over x plus one, divided by the fraction x plus three over x squared minus one,.
What is the first step in working out the fraction eigh over b, divided by the fraction c over d,?

Key idea: find a denominator that both denominators go into, multiply each numerator by the same thing as its denominator, then add or subtract the numerators. When you subtract, put the whole numerator in a bracket so the minus sign reaches every term.
Write the fraction three over x, plus the fraction two over x, as a single fraction.
Write the fraction x over five, plus the fraction two x over five, as a single fraction.
Write the fraction one over x, plus the fraction one over four, as a single fraction.
Write the fraction x plus one over two, plus the fraction x plus two over three, as a single fraction.
Write the fraction x plus one over two, minus the fraction x minus one over three, as a single fraction.
Write the fraction one over two, plus the fraction x plus three over x, minus the fraction one over x, as a single fraction. (Tip: combine the two terms with x in the denominator first.)
Key idea: leave the denominator factorised, and expand only the numerator. Then check whether the numerator factorises and cancels with the denominator.
Write the fraction one over x plus one, plus the fraction one over x plus two, as a single fraction.
Write the fraction two over x minus one, minus the fraction one over x plus one, as a single fraction.
Write the fraction x over x squared minus four, plus the fraction one over x plus two, as a single fraction. (Factorise the first denominator.)
Key idea: multiply every term by the common denominator. If x ends up in the denominator, you may get an x squared term. Then it is a Quadratic: move everything to one side and factorise.
Solve the fraction x over three, plus the fraction x over four, equals seven.
Solve the fraction x plus one over two, equals the fraction x plus four over five,.
Solve the fraction six over x, equals three.
Solve the fraction two over x plus one, equals the fraction one over x minus two,.
Solve x plus the fraction six over x, equals five. Type the two answers like one,7.
Solve x equals the fraction four over x,. Type the two answers like three,-three.
Key idea: the rate of a job that takes t hours is the fraction one over t, per hour. Rates add. The time together is the reciprocal of the combined rate.

Pipe eigh fills a tank in four hours. Pipe B fills it in twelve hours. How many hours do they take together? The picture shows: A tank with two pipes feeding it. One pipe is labelled eigh: four hours alone. The other is labelled B: twelve hours alone.
Painter eigh paints a room in five hours. Painter B paints it in twenty hours. How many hours do they take working together?

Pipe eigh fills a tank in x hours. Pipe B fills it in (x plus three) hours. Write their combined rate, in tanks per hour, as a single fraction. The picture shows: A tank with two pipes feeding it. One pipe is labelled eigh: x hours alone. The other is labelled B: x plus three hours alone.

Pipe eigh fills a tank in x hours. Pipe B fills it in (x plus five) hours. Together they fill it in six hours, so the fraction one over x, plus the fraction one over x plus five, equals the fraction one over six,. Solve this to find x, the time for pipe eigh on its own, in hours.

Key idea: in a show that question the answer is given to you. The marks are for the working that gets there. Use a common denominator, expand the numerator carefully, and finish by saying as required.
Show that the fraction x squared minus one over x plus one, plus one equals x.
Show that the fraction one over x minus one, minus the fraction one over x, equals the fraction one over x(x minus one),.

The sum of the reciprocals of the whole numbers n and n plus one is the fraction two n plus one over n(n plus one),. Use this to work out the sum of the reciprocals of three and four. Type it like five over eight.
Key idea: splitting and combining undo each other. Check one by doing the other.
Write two plus the fraction one over x, as a single fraction.
Write three plus the fraction two over x, as a single fraction.
Write the fraction five x plus two over x, as a number plus a fraction. Type it like four plus three/x.
Write the fraction one over two, plus the fraction one over x, as a single fraction.
Write x plus three as a fraction with a denominator of (x plus two). Do not simplify it.
Which is the same as the fraction six x plus nine over three,?
Dee says: the fraction x plus five over x, equals five, because the x in the numerator cancels with the x in the denominator. What went wrong?
Eli says: the fraction one over x, plus the fraction one over three, equals the fraction two over x plus three,. What went wrong?
Fay says: the fraction x squared minus nine over x minus three, equals x minus three, because x squared minus nine equals (x minus three) squared. What went wrong?
Gus says: the fraction x over two, minus the fraction x minus one over three, equals the fraction three x minus two x minus one over six, equals the fraction x minus one over six,. What went wrong?
Simplify the fraction two x plus six over x plus three,.
Write the fraction x plus one over three, plus the fraction x minus one over three, as a single fraction in its simplest form.
Solve the fraction five over x, equals two. Give your answer as a decimal.
Work out the fraction x over two, times the fraction six over x squared,.
Simplify the fraction x squared plus five x plus six over x plus two,.
Simplify fully the fraction x squared minus sixteen over x squared plus x minus twelve,. Type it like (x plus one)/(x-two).
Write the fraction one over x plus two, plus the fraction two over x minus one, as a single fraction. Type it like (two x plus one)/((x plus one)(x-three)).
Solve x minus three equals the fraction ten over x,. Type the two answers like three,-one.
Show that the fraction one over n, minus the fraction one over n plus two, equals the fraction two over n(n plus two),.

Ben can paint a fence in x hours. Cara can paint it in (x plus six) hours. Working together they take four hours. So the fraction one over x, plus the fraction one over x plus six, equals the fraction one over four,. Work out x.
Simplify fully the fraction x squared minus four over x plus three, divided by the fraction x plus two over x squared minus nine,. Type it like (x plus one)(x-four).
Solve x plus the fraction one over x, equals two. Type the value of x.

Show that the fraction one over n, minus the fraction one over n plus one, equals the fraction one over n(n plus one),. Then use the result to explain why the fraction one over one times two, plus the fraction one over two times three, plus the fraction one over three times four, equals the fraction three over four,.

Use the same idea to work out the fraction one over one times two, plus the fraction one over two times three, plus the fraction one over three times four, plus the fraction one over four times five,. Type it like three over four.

An electrician wires two resistors in parallel, one of six ohms and one of twelve ohms. The total resistance R in ohms follows the fraction one over R, equals the fraction one over six, plus the fraction one over twelve,. Work out R, in ohms.

Two resistors of ten ohms and fifteen ohms are wired in parallel. Use the fraction one over R, equals the fraction one over ten, plus the fraction one over fifteen, to find the total resistance R, in ohms.

A plumber fills a water tank using two pipes. Pipe eigh alone takes twelve hours and pipe B alone takes six hours. How many hours do they take together? The picture shows: A tank with two pipes feeding it. One pipe is labelled eigh: twelve hours alone. The other is labelled B: six hours alone.

A carpenter and an apprentice fit a kitchen. The carpenter would take six days alone and the apprentice would take three days alone. Each is paid two hundred pounds a day. How much does the labour cost when they work together? Give your answer in pounds, like one hundred and twenty.

An electrician has two resistors in parallel. One is x ohms. The other is two x ohms. The total resistance is four ohms. So the fraction one over x, plus the fraction one over two x, equals the fraction one over four,. Work out x.
A plumber fills a cistern with two pipes. Pipe eigh takes x hours alone. Pipe B takes (x plus three) hours alone. Together they take two hours. Find x, the time for pipe eigh alone, in hours.

Units and money Length: cm, m. Area: cm squared, m squared. Volume: cm cubed, m cubed. one metre equals one hundred centimetres, so one metre squared equals ten thousand centimetres squared. one metre cubed equals one million centimetres cubed, and one thousand centimetres cubed equals one litre. Round money to two decimal places. Round UP when you buy things by the box, tin or length.
Work out twenty-four times fifteen.
Two angles in a triangle are fifty degrees and sixty degrees. What is the third angle? Answer in degrees.
Which shape has four equal sides and four right angles?
Key idea: perimeter is the distance round the outside, so it is a LENGTH. Count every side, including the ones the picture does not label (opposite sides of a rectangle are equal).
What is the perimeter of this rectangle? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A rectangle. The long sides are eight centimetres and the short sides are three centimetres.
A square patio has sides of seven metres. What is its perimeter? Answer in m. The picture shows: A square with one side labelled seven metres.

What is the perimeter of this triangle? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A triangle. The bottom side is seven centimetres, the left side is five point five centimetres and the right side is four point five centimetres.
A garden is a rectangle fifteen metres long and nine metres wide. Fencing goes all the way round the edge except for a gate gap two metres wide. How many metres of fencing are needed?

A room is four point two metres by three point five metres. A carpenter fits skirting board (the wooden strip along the bottom of a wall) round the walls except across a zero point nine metre door gap. How many metres of skirting board does she need?
A rectangle has a perimeter of thirty centimetres. Which pair could be its length and width?
Key idea: area is measured in SQUARE units: cm squared, m squared. Perimeter is a length (cm, m). Two shapes can have the same perimeter and different areas.

Each small square is one centimetre squared. What is the area of the shaded shape? Answer in cm squared. The picture shows: A grid of small squares, four across and three down, all shaded. Each small square is one centimetre by one centimetre.
A rectangle is nine centimetres long and five centimetres wide. What is its area? Answer in cm squared. The picture shows: A rectangle with length nine centimetres and width five centimetres.
A square has sides of six centimetres. What is its area? Answer in cm squared.
A rectangle is seven metres by four metres. What is its area?
A lawn is twelve point five metres long and eight metres wide. What is its area? Answer in m squared.
A rectangle measures ten centimetres by two centimetres. A square has a side of six centimetres. Both have a perimeter of twenty-four centimetres. Which has the bigger area?
A tabletop is one point two metres long and zero point eight metres wide. What is its area? Answer in m squared.
Key idea: always use the PERPENDICULAR height (the dashed line in the pictures, at a right angle to the base). The slanting sides are a trap: do not use them.

What is the area of this triangle? Answer in cm squared. The picture shows: A triangle with a base of fourteen centimetres. A dashed line at a right angle from the top corner down to the base is twelve centimetres. The slanting sides are thirteen centimetres and fifteen centimetres.
A triangle has a base of seven metres and a perpendicular height of six metres. What is its area? Answer in m squared.
A boat sail is a triangle with a base of three point two metres and a height of four point five metres (measured at right angles to the base). What is its area? Answer in m squared.

What is the area of this triangle? Answer in cm squared. The picture shows: A triangle with a base of ten centimetres. The two equal slanting sides are each thirteen centimetres. A dashed line at a right angle from the top corner to the base is twelve centimetres.

This triangle has a right angle. What is its area? Answer in cm squared. The picture shows: A right-angled triangle. The two sides next to the right angle are nine centimetres along the bottom and six centimetres going up.

What is the area of this parallelogram? Answer in cm squared. The picture shows: A parallelogram with a base of eleven centimetres. A dashed line at a right angle from the top edge to the base is six centimetres. The slanting side is seven centimetres.

What is the area of this trapezium? Answer in cm squared. The picture shows: A trapezium. The top side is four centimetres and the bottom side is eight centimetres, and they are parallel. The dashed height between them is five centimetres.
The side of a shed is a trapezium. The two parallel sides are two point zero metres and two point four metres, and they are three metres apart. What is the area of the side? Answer in m squared.
A trapezium has parallel sides of nine centimetres and fifteen centimetres. They are seven centimetres apart. What is its area? Answer in cm squared.
Which is the formula for the area of a trapezium?

All the corners are right angles. What is the area of this shape? Answer in cm squared. The picture shows: An L shape with right-angle corners. The bottom is eight centimetres, the left side is six centimetres, the right side is three centimetres and the top is three centimetres.

This is the same shape as in the last question. What is its perimeter? Answer in cm. The picture shows: An L shape with right-angle corners. The bottom is eight centimetres, the left side is six centimetres, the right side is three centimetres and the top is three centimetres.
A lawn is twelve metres by nine metres. In it there is a square pond with sides of three metres. How many square metres of grass are there? Answer in m squared.

A picture frame is thirty centimetres by twenty centimetres on the outside. The picture inside is twenty-four centimetres by fourteen centimetres. What is the area of the wooden frame itself? Answer in cm squared. The picture shows: A rectangular frame, thirty centimetres by twenty centimetres on the outside, with a picture twenty-four centimetres by fourteen centimetres in the middle. The wooden border round the picture is white.

The end wall of a house is a rectangle with a triangle on top. How many square metres of wall will be painted? The picture shows: A house end wall. The rectangle part is six metres wide and four metres high. A triangle on top has the same six metres base. A dashed line shows the triangle height, two metres.
How do you find the area of a T-shape?

Key idea: to change m squared to cm squared, multiply by ten thousand. To change cm squared to m squared, divide by ten thousand. Or avoid the problem: change all the lengths to the same unit BEFORE you multiply.
How many square centimetres are in one square metre? Type it like five thousand.
Change three metres squared to cm squared. Type it like five thousand.
Change forty-five thousand centimetres squared to m squared.
A rectangle is three metres long and forty centimetres wide. What is its area in m squared?
A rectangle is eighty centimetres long and one point five metres wide. What is its area in cm squared? Type it like five thousand.
Which is bigger, two metres squared or fifteen thousand centimetres squared?
Key idea: round UP when you buy things in whole boxes or tins, even if the next digit is small. Rounding down leaves you short.
A lawn is nine metres by six metres. Turf (grass sold in rolls) costs five pounds fifty per m squared. How much does the turf for the lawn cost? Type it like twelve point five zero.

A room is four point five metres by three point six metres. Laminate flooring costs fourteen pounds fifty per m squared. What does it cost to cover the whole floor? Type it like twelve point five zero.
A wall to be tiled is five point four metres squared. Each box of tiles covers two metres squared. How many boxes must be bought?
A wall is six metres long and two point five metres high. It needs two coats of paint. One litre covers ten metres squared in one coat. How many litres are needed?

A kitchen wall three point six metres wide and two point five metres high is tiled. Boxes of tiles cover one point five metres squared and cost twenty-nine pounds fifty a box. How much do the tiles cost? Type it like twelve point five zero.
A patio is four metres by three point five metres. It is covered with square slabs, each fifty centimetres by fifty centimetres. How many slabs are needed?

Key idea: volume equals area of cross-section times length works for every prism. First find the area of the flat end, then multiply by the length. Remember that one metre cubed equals one hundred times one hundred times one hundred equals one million centimetres cubed. And one thousand centimetres cubed equals one litre.
What is the volume of this cuboid? Answer in cm cubed. The picture shows: A box shape. The length is six centimetres, the width is four centimetres and the height is three centimetres.
A cuboid is five centimetres by four centimetres by two centimetres. What is its surface area? Answer in cm squared.

This prism has a right-angled triangle for its cross-section. The triangle has a base of five centimetres and a height of four centimetres. The prism is eight centimetres long. What is its volume? Answer in cm cubed. The picture shows: A solid with a right-angled triangle at the front, with a base of five centimetres and a height of four centimetres. The solid runs back eight centimetres.
A fish tank is sixty centimetres long, thirty centimetres wide and forty centimetres high. What is its volume? Answer in cm cubed. Type it like five thousand.
one thousand centimetres cubed is the same as one litre. The fish tank has a volume of seventy-two thousand centimetres cubed. How many litres of water can it hold when it is full?

A path is twelve metres long, one point five metres wide and zero point one metres thick, made of concrete. Concrete costs one hundred and twenty-five pounds per m cubed. How much does the concrete cost? Type it like twelve point five zero.
Which unit is used for volume?
Key idea: write the formula with the numbers you know, then ask: what must I multiply by six to get fifty-four? Undo the multiplication with a division. Then check by going forwards.
A rectangle has an area of fifty-four centimetres squared and a width of six centimetres. What is its length? Answer in cm.
A square lawn has an area of sixty-four metres squared. How many metres of edging go all the way round it?
A rectangle has a perimeter of thirty-six centimetres and a length of eleven centimetres. What is its width? Answer in cm.
A triangle has an area of twenty-four centimetres squared and a base of eight centimetres. What is its perpendicular height? Answer in cm.
A parallelogram has an area of seventy-two centimetres squared and a perpendicular height of eight centimetres. What is its base? Answer in cm.
A trapezium has an area of forty-five centimetres squared. Its parallel sides are four centimetres and eleven centimetres. How far apart are they? Answer in cm.
A cuboid has a volume of two hundred and forty centimetres cubed. It is ten centimetres long and six centimetres wide. How high is it? Answer in cm.
Laminate flooring costs sixteen pounds per m squared. A customer has four hundred and eighty pounds to spend on it. What is the largest area it can cover? Answer in m squared.

From L1 the ship is on a bearing of zero four five degrees and from L2 it is on a bearing of three hundred and fifteen degrees.

A boat leaves a port P and sails twelve kilometres on a bearing of zero six zero degrees to B. It then sails five kilometres on a bearing of one hundred and fifty degrees to C. Work out the bearing of the port P from C. Give your answer to one decimal place. The picture shows: A path from port P to B and then B to C with a right angle at B. P to B is twelve kilometres on a bearing of zero six zero degrees, and B to C is five kilometres on a bearing of one hundred and fifty degrees. A dashed line joins P to C.

Typing and rounding Bounds are numbers, so type them in full, like two point three five or four thousand, two hundred and fifty. Do not round a bound unless the question says so. Type an error interval with is less than and is less than equals, using the letter in the question, like two point three five is less than equals x is less than two point four five. Type is less than equals for is less than or equal to. The answer box also accepts the is less than or equal to sign if you paste it. Spaces do not matter. Keep the full calculator value in a calculation, and round only at the end.
Round three point four six to one decimal place.
Round three thousand, eight hundred and sixty-two to the nearest one hundred.
Round zero point zero three six seven to two significant figures.
x is an integer and two is less than or equal to x is less than six. List the values of x. Put commas between them, like one,2,3.
Key idea: half the rounding unit, below and above. The most common slip is to use the whole unit, or half of the wrong unit.
A mass is sixty-two kilograms, to the nearest kg. What is its lower bound, in kg?
A crowd is three thousand, four hundred to the nearest one hundred. What is its upper bound?
A pipe is one point eight metres long, to one decimal place. What is its lower bound, in m?
A reading is twelve point four five volts, to two decimal places. What is its upper bound, in volts?
A distance is four thousand, three hundred metres, to two significant figures. What is its lower bound, in m?
A length is nine point zero centimetres to one decimal place. What is its upper bound?
Key idea: error interval: lower bound is less than or equal to x is less than upper bound. Include the lower bound, leave out the upper bound.

x equals seven, to the nearest whole number. Write the error interval for x. Type it like two point five is less than equals x is less than three point five. The picture shows: A number line from five to nine with a point marked at seven.
A length is l equals two point four metres, to one decimal place. Write the error interval for l.
n equals five hundred and sixty, to two significant figures. Write the error interval for n.
t equals zero point zero eight five, to two significant figures. Write the error interval for t.
A mass is m equals fifteen kilograms, to the nearest five kilograms. Write the error interval for m.
A cable is cut to l equals three point six zero metres, correct to the nearest centimetre. Write the error interval for l, in metres.

Key idea: truncating cuts digits off, so the true number is at least the truncated number and below one whole unit more. Rounding goes half a unit each way. Truncating goes a whole unit up, and none down.
x equals five point two, truncated to one decimal place. Write the error interval for x.
A number is twelve after it has been truncated to a whole number. What is the smallest it could be?
A number is twelve after it has been truncated to a whole number. What is its upper bound?
A number is three point four when truncated to one decimal place. Which error interval is correct?
A stopwatch shows fourteen point eight seconds, truncated to one decimal place. Write the error interval for the real time t.

Key idea: for eigh minus b, to make the answer as big as possible you start with the biggest a and take away the smallest b. To make it as small as possible, take away the biggest b from the smallest a.
eigh equals eight and b equals five, both to the nearest whole number. What is the greatest possible value of eigh plus b?
eigh equals eight and b equals five, both to the nearest whole number. What is the smallest possible value of eigh plus b?
p equals twenty point four and q equals seven point nine, both to one decimal place. What is the greatest possible value of p minus q?
p equals twenty point four and q equals seven point nine, both to one decimal place. What is the smallest possible value of p minus q?
Two lengths of conduit are one point two metres, to one decimal place, and zero point eight five metres, to two decimal places. What is the greatest possible total length, in m?
A pipe is two point five metres long, to one decimal place. A piece zero point eight metres long, to one decimal place, is cut off. What is the smallest possible length left, in m?
Key idea: to make a division eigh divided by b as big as possible, divide the biggest a by the smallest b. To make it as small as possible, divide the smallest a by the biggest b.

A tile is twenty centimetres by ten centimetres, both to the nearest cm. What is the greatest possible area, in cm squared? The picture shows: A rectangle for the tile, with its length of twenty centimetres along the top and its width of ten centimetres down the side.
A tile is twenty centimetres by ten centimetres, both to the nearest cm. What is the smallest possible area, in cm squared?

A rectangle is six point four centimetres by three point two centimetres, both to one decimal place. What is the smallest possible perimeter, in cm? The picture shows: A rectangle with its length of six point four centimetres along the top and its width of three point two centimetres down the side.
x equals fifteen and y equals four, both to the nearest whole number. What is the greatest possible value of x divided by y? Give your answer to two decimal places.
x equals fifteen and y equals four, both to the nearest whole number. What is the smallest possible value of x divided by y? Give your answer to two decimal places.

A twenty-four point five metre cable, to one decimal place, is cut into pieces of three point five metres, to one decimal place. What is the greatest possible value of twenty-four point five divided by three point five? Give your answer to two decimal places.

Key idea: look at the formula. A quantity that is divided (the distance in distance divided by time) makes the answer bigger when it is bigger. A quantity you divide by (the time) makes the answer smaller when it is bigger.
A runner covers one hundred metres, to the nearest metre, in twelve point five s, to one decimal place. What is the greatest possible speed? Give your answer to two decimal places, in m/s.
A runner covers one hundred metres, to the nearest metre, in twelve point five s, to one decimal place. What is the smallest possible speed? Give your answer to two decimal places, in m/s.

The density of a metal is mass divided by volume. A block has mass four hundred and eighty grams, to the nearest ten grams, and volume sixty centimetres cubed, to the nearest cm cubed. What is the greatest possible density? Give your answer to two decimal places, in g/cm cubed.
A square has sides of four point five centimetres, to one decimal place. What is the upper bound of its area, in cm squared?

A journey is one hundred and fifty kilometres, to the nearest ten kilometres, at sixty kilometres/h, to the nearest ten kilometres/h. What is the greatest possible time? Give your answer to two decimal places, in hours.
Key idea: if the upper bound and lower bound round to the same value, the true answer must round to that value too. Any more figures would be a guess.

A bike travels three hundred and twenty metres, to the nearest metre, in sixteen point zero s, to one decimal place. The bounds of its speed are nineteen point nine zero six, and twenty point zero nine four, m/s. What is the speed to a degree of accuracy you can justify, in m/s?

A drone flies three hundred metres, to the nearest metre, in twelve point five s, to one decimal place. Work out the upper and lower bounds of its speed, then give the speed to a degree of accuracy you can justify, in m/s.

A delivery robot moves twenty-four metres, to the nearest metre, in four point eight minutes, to one decimal place. Its speed is twenty-four divided by four point eight equals five metres/min. The upper and lower bounds are five point one five eight, and four point eight four five, m/min. What speed can you justify? Answer to the number of significant figures the bounds allow.

A metal block has mass four hundred and eighty grams, to the nearest ten grams, and volume sixty centimetres cubed, to the nearest cm cubed. The bounds of its density are seven point eight five, and eight point one five, g/cm cubed. What density can you justify?
The bounds of a speed are nineteen point nine, and twenty point zero nine, m/s. Why is giving the speed as twenty point zero metres/s not justified?
Key idea: number equals the middle of the interval. Rounding unit equals upper bound minus lower bound.
A number has the error interval three point four five is less than or equal to x is less than three point five five. It was rounded to one decimal place. What is the number?
A number has a lower bound of two thousand, four hundred and fifty and an upper bound of two thousand, five hundred and fifty. It was rounded to the nearest one hundred. What is the number?
A number has the error interval zero point one seven five is less than or equal to x is less than zero point one eight five. What is the number, rounded to two decimal places?
The upper bound of a number is eight point three five. It was rounded to one decimal place. What is the number?
x is a number rounded to one decimal place. The upper bound of two x is nine point one. What is x?
A length has the error interval fourteen point five is less than or equal to l is less than fifteen point five, in metres. How was it rounded?
Tom says: a length of five point four centimetres, to one decimal place, has an upper bound of five point five centimetres. What went wrong?
Ava says: the greatest possible value of eigh minus b is the upper bound of a minus the upper bound of b. What went wrong?
Ben says: the error interval for twelve, to the nearest whole number, is eleven point five is less than x is less than or equal to twelve point five. What went wrong?
x equals zero point six, to one decimal place. Write the error interval for x.
eigh equals three point five and b equals two point one, both to one decimal place. What is the greatest possible value of eigh plus b?
eigh equals three point five and b equals two point one, both to one decimal place. What is the smallest possible value of eigh times b?
A number is nine point four after being truncated to one decimal place. What is its upper bound?
eigh equals three point five and b equals two point one, both to one decimal place. What is the greatest possible value of eigh divided by b? Give your answer to two decimal places.
eigh equals three point five and b equals two point one, both to one decimal place. What is the smallest possible value of eigh minus b?
A cable is twelve point five metres long, correct to one decimal place. Three of these cables are laid end to end. Work out the upper bound of the total length, in m.

A rectangle is six point four centimetres long and three point two centimetres wide, both to one decimal place. Work out the lower bound of its area. Give your answer to two decimal places, in cm squared.
A runner covers four hundred metres, to the nearest ten metres, in fifty-two s, to the nearest second. Work out the speed to a degree of accuracy that is justified. Give your answer in m/s.

A rod is two point four metres long, to one decimal place. Pieces of zero point three five metres, to two decimal places, are cut from it. Show that it might be possible to cut seven pieces from the rod. The picture shows: A long bar for the rod, with a short piece at its left end the size of one cut piece.
p equals four point eight, to one decimal place, and q equals zero point two five, to two decimal places. Work out the upper bound of p divided by q. Give your answer to three significant figures.

A square tile has sides of fifteen centimetres, to the nearest cm. Show that the area of the tile cannot be less than two hundred and ten centimetres squared. The picture shows: A square tile with each side marked fifteen centimetres.
A length is five metres, to the nearest metre. Maya says: Twice the length must be ten metres, to the nearest metre. Show that Maya might be wrong.

A number x is four point five when rounded to one decimal place, and five when rounded to one significant figure. Write the error interval for all the values of x that fit both facts. Type it like one is less than equals x is less than two.

eigh equals seven point two and b equals three point one, both to one decimal place. Work out the upper bound of eigh divided by (eigh minus b). Give your answer to three significant figures. (Take care: a appears twice, so the usual rule does not work.)

An electrician measures a cable run as twenty-four metres, to the nearest metre. Cable costs one pounds ninety per metre. What is the greatest the cable could cost? Give your answer to two decimal places, like twelve point five zero.
A copper pipe has an outside diameter of d equals fifteen millimetres, to the nearest millimetre. Write the error interval for d.

A carpenter has a board two point four zero metres long, to the nearest centimetre. She cuts shelves zero point six zero metres long, to the nearest centimetre. What is the smallest possible value of the board length divided by the shelf length? Give your answer to three significant figures. Can she be certain of getting four shelves?

A bolt has diameter eleven point eight millimetres, to one decimal place, and fits in a hole of diameter twelve point zero millimetres, to one decimal place. What is the smallest possible gap between the bolt and the hole, in mm?

The current in a circuit is I equals V divided by R. The voltage V is two hundred and thirty V, to the nearest ten V, and the resistance R is forty-six ohms, to the nearest ohm. Work out the current to a degree of accuracy that is justified, in amps.

A plumber fills a tank of one hundred and fifty litres, to the nearest ten litres, using a pump that delivers twelve litres per minute, to the nearest litre per minute. What is the greatest possible time to fill the tank? Give your answer to one decimal place, in minutes.

How to write a reason In an exam, the answer and the reason are marked separately. The reason is usually a C1 mark: it is lost if you write only the angle. Write the angle you found, then a short reason in words, using the standard wording. Not it is a circle rule or same arc. Say the whole fact. You will also use simpler reasons: angles in a triangle add up to one hundred and eighty degrees, angles on a straight line add up to one hundred and eighty degrees, angles in a quadrilateral add up to three hundred and sixty degrees, and the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal (two radii make an isosceles triangle). Angles can be written with three letters. Angle ACB is the angle at C between the lines to eigh and to B.
An isosceles triangle has an angle of fifty degrees at the top. What is each base angle? Answer in degrees.
Three angles of a quadrilateral are ninety degrees, one hundred and five degrees and eighty-five degrees. What is the fourth angle? Answer in degrees.
A right-angled triangle has two short sides of five centimetres and twelve centimetres. How long is the longest side? Answer in cm.
A circle has a diameter of eighteen centimetres. What is its radius? Answer in cm.
Key idea: almost every theorem is about two things: which points are on the circle, and which arc the angle stands on. Always find the arc first.
A straight line touches a circle at exactly one point. What is it called?
What is the region between a chord and the arc it cuts off called?

Look at the picture. Which angle is the angle at the centre? The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh and B. A point C on the circle also joins to eigh and B.
Which is the longest chord of a circle?
Theorem one: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, when both stand on the same arc.

Key idea: the corner of the angle must be on the circle (for the circumference) or at O (for the centre). If C is on the short arc AB, the angle at the centre it goes with is the reflex angle, three hundred and sixty degrees minus AOB.

O is the centre of the circle. Angle ACB equals thirty-eight degrees. Work out angle AOB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh and B. A point C on the circle also joins to eigh and B.

O is the centre of the circle. Angle AOB equals one hundred and thirty degrees. Work out angle ACB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh and B. A point C on the circle also joins to eigh and B.

Angle AOB equals one hundred and twenty-four degrees and angle ACB equals sixty-two degrees. Give a reason why angle ACB equals sixty-two degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh and B. A point C on the circle also joins to eigh and B.

O is the centre of the circle. Angle AOB equals one hundred and thirty degrees. Work out angle OAB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh, O to B and eigh to B, making a triangle.

O is the centre of the circle. Angle AOB equals (five x plus ten) degrees and angle ACB equals (two x plus fifteen) degrees. Work out x. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh and B. A point C on the circle also joins to eigh and B.
The angle at the circumference is forty-one degrees. What is the angle at the centre when both stand on the same arc? Answer in degrees.

O is the centre. Angle AOB equals one hundred degrees. The point C is on the SHORT arc AB. Work out angle ACB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh and B. A point C on the circle also joins to eigh and B.
Theorem two: angles in the same segment are equal. (Angles at the circumference that stand on the same arc are equal.)

C and D are on the circle. Angle ACB equals forty-two degrees. Work out angle ADB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with chord AB near the top. Points C and D on the lower part of the circle are each joined to eigh and to B.

C and D are in the same segment. Angle ACB equals (two x plus five) degrees and angle ADB equals (four x minus twenty-one) degrees. Work out x. The picture shows: A circle with chord AB near the top. Points C and D on the lower part of the circle are each joined to eigh and to B.

Angle ACB equals fifty-five degrees and angle ADB equals fifty-five degrees. Give a reason why these two angles are equal. The picture shows: A circle with chord AB near the top. Points C and D on the lower part of the circle are each joined to eigh and to B.
Angle ACB equals three x degrees and angle ADB equals (x plus forty) degrees, where C and D are in the same segment. Work out x.

Angle ACB equals sixty-two degrees. Which angle must also be sixty-two degrees? The picture shows: A circle with chord AB near the top. Points C and D on the lower part of the circle are each joined to eigh and to B. A point E at the top of the circle, on the other side of the chord, is also joined to eigh and to B.
Theorem three: the angle in a semicircle is ninety degrees. (The angle at the circumference, standing on a diameter.)

AB is a diameter of the circle. Angle CAB equals thirty-five degrees. Work out angle ABC. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with a diameter AB across it through the centre O. Point C is on the circle above, joined to eigh and to B.

AB is a diameter of a circle and is ten centimetres long. The point C is on the circle and AC equals six centimetres. How long is BC? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A circle with a diameter AB across it through the centre O. Point C is on the circle above, joined to eigh and to B.

AB is a diameter. Give a reason why angle ACB equals ninety degrees. The picture shows: A circle with a diameter AB across it through the centre O. Point C is on the circle above, joined to eigh and to B.

AB is a diameter. Angle CAB equals three x degrees and angle CBA equals two x degrees. Work out x. The picture shows: A circle with a diameter AB across it through the centre O. Point C is on the circle above, joined to eigh and to B.
A triangle ABC has all three corners on a circle. The angle at C is ninety degrees. What must be true about AB?
Theorem four: the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to one hundred and eighty degrees.

ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle DAB equals one hundred and five degrees. Work out angle BCD. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with four points eigh, B, C and D on it in order. Straight lines join them to make a four-sided shape.

ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle ABC equals eighty-eight degrees. Work out angle ADC. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with four points eigh, B, C and D on it in order. Straight lines join them to make a four-sided shape.

ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle DAB equals (two x plus ten) degrees and angle BCD equals (three x minus twenty) degrees. Work out x. The picture shows: A circle with four points eigh, B, C and D on it in order. Straight lines join them to make a four-sided shape.

ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. The side AB is extended to E. Angle ADC equals seventy-two degrees. Work out the exterior angle CBE. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with four points eigh, B, C and D on it in order. Straight lines join them to make a four-sided shape.

Angle ABC equals eighty-eight degrees and angle ADC equals ninety-two degrees. Give a reason why these two angles add up to one hundred and eighty degrees. The picture shows: A circle with four points eigh, B, C and D on it in order. Straight lines join them to make a four-sided shape.

O is the centre of the circle. Angle BOD equals one hundred and forty degrees. eigh is on the long arc BD and C is on the short arc BD. Work out angle BCD. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. Points B and D are at the top left and top right. eigh is at the bottom and C is at the top. Lines join eigh, B, C and D in order, and O is joined to B and to D.
Theorem five: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The angle between them is ninety degrees.
Theorem six: two tangents drawn to a circle from the same outside point are equal in length.

TA is a tangent at eigh to a circle with centre O. Angle OTA equals twenty-eight degrees. Work out angle AOT. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside has a straight line TA that touches the circle at eigh, and a dashed line TO to the centre. A right-angle square is at eigh.

A circle has a radius of five centimetres. T is thirteen centimetres from the centre O. TA is a tangent to the circle at eigh. How long is TA? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside has a straight line TA touching the circle at eigh, and a dashed line TO to the centre. A right-angle square is at eigh. Not to scale.

TA and TB are tangents to the circle. Angle ATB equals fifty degrees. Work out angle TAB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside the circle has two straight lines drawn from it, each touching the circle at one point, eigh and B.

TA and TB are tangents to the circle with centre O. Angle ATB equals fifty degrees. Work out angle AOB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside the circle has two straight lines drawn from it, each touching the circle at one point, eigh and B.

TA and TB are tangents to the circle. Give a reason why TA equals TB. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside the circle has two straight lines drawn from it, each touching the circle at one point, eigh and B.
TA and TB are tangents to a circle from T. TA equals (three x plus two) cm and TB equals (five x minus six) cm. How long is TA? Answer in cm.

TA is a tangent at eigh and O is the centre. Which angle is ninety degrees? The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside has a straight line TA touching the circle at eigh, and a dashed line TO to the centre.
Theorem seven: the angle between a tangent and a chord is equal to the angle in the alternate segment.

TS is a tangent to the circle at eigh. Angle SAB equals fifty-two degrees. Work out angle ACB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with a straight line TS touching it at the bottom point eigh. A chord AB goes up to the right of eigh. A third point C on the circle is joined to eigh and to B.

TS is a tangent to the circle at eigh. Angle ACB equals sixty-four degrees. Work out angle TAB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with a straight line TS touching it at the bottom point eigh. A chord AB goes up to the right of eigh. A third point C on the circle is joined to eigh and to B.

Angle SAB equals fifty-two degrees and angle ACB equals fifty-two degrees. Give a reason why these angles are equal. The picture shows: A circle with a straight line TS touching it at the bottom point eigh. A chord AB goes up to the right of eigh. A third point C on the circle is joined to eigh and to B.

TS is a tangent at eigh. Angle SAB equals forty-eight degrees and angle CAB equals sixty-two degrees. Work out angle ABC. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with a straight line TS touching it at the bottom point eigh. A chord AB goes up to the right of eigh. A third point C on the circle is joined to eigh and to B.

TS is a tangent at eigh. Angle SAB equals (three x plus ten) degrees and angle ACB equals (five x minus twenty) degrees. Work out x. The picture shows: A circle with a straight line TS touching it at the bottom point eigh. A chord AB goes up to the right of eigh. A third point C on the circle is joined to eigh and to B.

In the picture, which angle is in the alternate segment to angle SAB? The picture shows: A circle with a straight line TS touching it at the bottom point eigh. A chord AB goes up to the right of eigh. A third point C on the circle is joined to eigh and to B.
Theorem eight: the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord. The line from the centre meets the chord at a right angle, at its midpoint.

The radius of the circle is thirteen centimetres and the chord AB is twenty-four centimetres. M is the midpoint of AB. How far is M from O? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A chord AB lies below the centre. A line from O meets the chord at M with a right angle.

The radius is ten centimetres. The chord AB is six centimetres from the centre O, measured at right angles to AB. How long is AB? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A chord AB lies below the centre. A line from O meets the chord at M with a right angle.

M is the midpoint of the chord AB and OM is perpendicular to AB. Give a reason why AM equals MB. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A chord AB lies below the centre. A line from O meets the chord at M with a right angle.

The radius is thirteen centimetres and the line OM from the centre is five centimetres. OM is perpendicular to the chord AB. How long is AB? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A chord AB lies below the centre. A line from O meets the chord at M with a right angle.
A line from the centre of a circle meets a chord at right angles. What else is always true?
A chord of twenty-four centimetres is five centimetres from the centre of a circle, measured at right angles to the chord. What is the radius of the circle? Answer in cm.
Key idea: work out ONE angle at a time, write its reason beside it, and mark each angle on the diagram as you go. Do not try to jump straight to the answer.

Angle AOB equals one hundred and twelve degrees and angle ACB equals fifty-six degrees, where O is the centre. Give a reason for angle ACB equals fifty-six degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh and B. A point C on the circle also joins to eigh and B.

TA is a tangent and O is the centre. Give a reason why angle OAT equals ninety degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside has a straight line TA touching the circle at eigh, and a dashed line TO to the centre.

ABCD is a quadrilateral with all four corners on a circle. Angle ABC equals one hundred degrees and angle ADC equals eighty degrees. Give a reason why angle ADC equals eighty degrees. The picture shows: A circle with four points eigh, B, C and D on it in order. Straight lines join them to make a four-sided shape.

Angle ACB equals forty degrees and angle ADB equals forty degrees. Give a reason why angle ADB equals forty degrees. The picture shows: A circle with chord AB near the top. Points C and D on the lower part of the circle are each joined to eigh and to B.

OA and OB are radii and angle AOB equals one hundred and thirty degrees. Give a reason why angle OAB equals angle OBA. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh, O to B and eigh to B, making a triangle.

AB is a diameter, and C is a point on the circle. Which reason shows that triangle ABC has a right angle at C? The picture shows: A circle with a diameter AB across it through the centre O. Point C is on the circle above, joined to eigh and to B.

TA and TB are tangents to the circle with centre O. Angle ATB equals forty degrees. Work out angle OAB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside the circle has two straight lines drawn from it, each touching the circle at one point, eigh and B.

AB is a diameter of the circle. C and D are on the circle, as shown. Angle CAB equals twenty-five degrees. Work out angle ADC. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with a diameter AB through the centre O. Point C is on the circle above and to the right, joined to eigh and B. Point D is at the bottom, joined to eigh and C.

TS is a tangent to the circle at eigh, and O is the centre. Angle SAB equals thirty-five degrees. Work out angle AOB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with a straight line TS touching it at the bottom point eigh. A chord AB goes up to the right of eigh. A third point C on the circle is joined to eigh and to B.

TA is a tangent to the circle with centre O. The line TO meets the circle at B. Angle ATO equals thirty degrees. Work out angle OAB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside on the left has a tangent TA touching the circle at eigh, and a line TO that crosses the circle at B before reaching O. A chord AB is drawn.

AB is a diameter of a circle and ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle ABD equals thirty degrees. Work out angle BCD. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with a diameter AB through the centre O. Points C and D are on the upper half of the circle. The four points eigh, B, C and D are joined in order to make a four-sided shape, and D is joined to B.
Key idea: to name the theorem, find the clue in the diagram first: a centre, a diameter, a tangent, or four points.

In the picture, angle AOB equals ninety-six degrees and angle ACB equals forty-eight degrees. Which theorem links them? The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh and B. A point C on the circle also joins to eigh and B.

In the picture, angle ACB is ninety degrees. Which theorem makes this true? The picture shows: A circle with a diameter AB across it through the centre O. Point C is on the circle above, joined to eigh and to B.

In the picture, angle eigh equals one hundred and five degrees and the angle at the opposite corner is seventy-five degrees. Which theorem makes them add to one hundred and eighty degrees? The picture shows: A circle with four points eigh, B, C and D on it in order. Straight lines join them to make a four-sided shape.

The two lines TA and TB touch the circle at eigh and B. Which theorem tells you TA equals TB? The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside the circle has two straight lines drawn from it, each touching the circle at one point, eigh and B.
A triangle has all three corners on a circle, and one side is a diameter. What do you know about the angle opposite that side?
Key idea: in a proof, every statement needs a reason. Finish by saying what you set out to show.

AB is a diameter of a circle with centre O, and C is a point on the circle. Prove that angle ACB equals ninety degrees. The picture shows: A circle with a diameter AB across it through the centre O. Point C is on the circle above, joined to eigh and to B.

ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral in a circle with centre O. Let angle BAD equals x. Prove that angle BCD equals one hundred and eighty degrees minus x. (Take x at most ninety degrees. Which theorem would you use first if the diagram shows a diameter?

O is the centre of a circle. Angle ACB equals fifty-four degrees, where C is on the long arc AB. Work out the reflex angle AOB (the angle at O that is bigger than one hundred and eighty degrees), on the long-arc side. Answer in degrees.
ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle ABC equals seventy-six degrees. The side AB is extended to E. Work out angle CBE. Answer in degrees.
A circle has a radius of eight point five centimetres. A chord is eight centimetres from the centre, measured at right angles to the chord. How long is the chord? Answer in cm.

A bricklayer builds an arch with a span (width) of two point four metres and a rise (height) of zero point five metres. The curve is part of a circle. Work out the radius of the circle. Give your answer in m. The picture shows: A flat base line with a curved arch above it. The width of the base is marked as the span, two point four metres, and the height at the middle is marked as the rise, zero point five metres.

A plumber fits a strap to a round pipe with a radius of fifty millimetres. The strap is fixed at a point T that is one hundred and thirty millimetres from the centre of the pipe. The strap runs straight from T to touch the pipe at eigh. How long is the straight part TA? Answer in mm.

An electrician sets up a circular lighting track with centre O. Lights are at eigh and B, and angle AOB equals one hundred and ten degrees. A camera is on the track at C. Work out the angle ACB that the camera sees. C is on the long arc AB. Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. Two lights eigh and B are near the top and a camera C is at the bottom. Lines join O to eigh and B, and C to eigh and B.

A carpenter tests a corner with a semicircular piece of plywood. Its straight edge is a diameter, one point two metres long. eigh and B are the two ends of the straight edge, and C is a point on the curved edge. AC equals zero point seven two metres. How long is BC? Answer in m.

A plumber checks the level of water in a round pipe with a radius of twenty-five millimetres. The surface of the water makes a chord that is forty-eight millimetres long. How far is the surface of the water from the centre of the pipe? Answer in mm. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A chord AB, the water surface, is below the centre. A line from O meets the chord at M with a right-angle square.

The arch in the first question (span two point four metres, radius one point six nine metres) has a curved oak trim fixed along the whole curve. The trim costs eighteen pounds fifty per metre. How much does the trim cost? Use the full calculator value until the end, then give your answer to two decimal places, like twelve point five zero.

O is the centre of the circle. Angle AOB equals one hundred and eighteen degrees. Work out the size of angle ACB. Give a reason for your answer. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh and B. A point C on the circle also joins to eigh and B.

TA and TB are tangents to a circle with centre O. Angle ATB equals sixty-four degrees. Work out the size of angle OAB. Give reasons for your working. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A point T outside the circle has two straight lines drawn from it, each touching the circle at one point, eigh and B.

TS is a tangent to the circle at eigh. Angle SAB equals forty-eight degrees and angle CAB equals sixty-two degrees. Work out the size of angle ABC. Give a reason for each step. The picture shows: A circle with a straight line TS touching it at the bottom point eigh. A chord AB goes up to the right of eigh. A third point C on the circle is joined to eigh and to B.

A circle has a radius of seventeen centimetres. The chord AB is sixteen centimetres long. Work out the distance from the centre of the circle to the chord AB. Give your answer in cm. The picture shows: A circle with centre O. A chord AB lies below the centre. A line from O meets the chord at M with a right angle.

O is the centre of the circle. Angle AOB equals one hundred and thirty degrees. Work out angle OAB. Give reasons for your answer. The picture shows: A circle with centre O and points eigh and B on it. Lines join O to eigh, O to B and eigh to B, making a triangle.
Two tangents are drawn to a circle of radius four centimetres from a point T. The angle between the tangents is sixty degrees. How far is T from the centre O? Answer in cm.
ABCD is a parallelogram with all four corners on a circle. Angle ABC equals x degrees. Work out x.
A circular arc has a chord of twelve centimetres and a rise (height of the arc above the chord) of two centimetres. What is the radius of the circle? Answer in cm.

Units and rounding pi is about three point one four one five nine. Use the pi button on your calculator, not three point one four, unless the question says so. Circumference is a length (cm, m). Area is in square units (cm squared, m squared). Volume is in cubic units (cm cubed, m cubed). Do not round until the last step. Then give the number of decimal places the question asks for. Money is two decimal places.
Work out six squared.
What is the area of a rectangle eight centimetres long and five centimetres wide? Answer in cm squared.
What is the square root of eighty-one?
Key idea: radius and diameter are easy to swap by accident. Before you use any circle formula, ask yourself: is the number I was given the radius or the diameter?
This circle has a diameter of eighteen centimetres. What is its radius? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A circle with a line across it through the centre, labelled eighteen centimetres.
A circle has a radius of six point five centimetres. What is its diameter? Answer in cm.
Which part of a circle goes from the centre to the edge?
A round pond has a radius of two point four metres. What is its diameter? Answer in m.
The longest chord of a circle goes through the centre. What is it called?

Key idea: a quick check: the circumference is a bit more than three times the diameter. If a circle has a diameter of ten centimetres and your circumference is six centimetres or sixty centimetres, something has gone wrong.
A circle has a diameter of twenty centimetres. Work out its circumference. Give your answer to one decimal place.
A circle has a radius of five metres. Work out its circumference to one decimal place.
This circle has a diameter of twelve centimetres. Work out its circumference to one decimal place. The picture shows: A circle with a line across it through the centre, labelled twelve centimetres.
A plumber winds tape once round a copper pipe with a diameter of twenty-two millimetres. How long is one turn of tape? Give your answer in mm to one decimal place.

A cable drum has a diameter of zero point eight metres. A cable goes round it twenty-five times (ignore the thickness of the cable). How long is the cable on the drum? Give your answer in m to one decimal place.
A round table has a radius of sixty-five centimetres. A strip of wood goes once round its edge. How long is the strip? Give your answer in cm to one decimal place.
A bicycle wheel has a diameter of zero point seven metres. How far does the bike travel when the wheel turns round once? Give your answer in m to one decimal place.
Which is the best estimate for the circumference of a circle with a diameter of ten centimetres?
Key idea: area uses the RADIUS squared. If you are given the diameter, halve it first. And square only the r, not the pi: work out r squared first, then multiply by pi.
A circle has a radius of five centimetres. Work out its area to one decimal place. Answer in cm squared.
A circle has a diameter of sixteen centimetres. Work out its area to one decimal place. Answer in cm squared.
What is the area of this circle? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm squared. The picture shows: A circle with a line from the centre to the edge, labelled nine point five centimetres.
A round table top has a diameter of one point two metres. What is its area? Give your answer to two decimal places, in m squared.
A round trampoline has a diameter of three metres. What is the area of its mat? Give your answer to two decimal places, in m squared.

A circular patio has a radius of two metres. Paving costs forty-two pounds per m squared. How much does the paving cost? Use the full value from your calculator until the end, then give your answer to two decimal places, like twelve point five zero.
Which is the formula for the area of a circle?

Key idea: the PERIMETER of a semicircle or a quarter circle also includes the straight edges. A semicircle has one straight edge, equal to the diameter. A quarter circle has two straight edges, each equal to the radius.

What is the area of this semicircle? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm squared. The picture shows: A semicircle sitting on its straight edge. The straight edge is labelled eight centimetres.

This is the same semicircle as in the last question. What is its perimeter? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm. The picture shows: A semicircle sitting on its straight edge. The straight edge is labelled eight centimetres.

What is the area of this quarter circle with a radius of ten centimetres? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm squared. The picture shows: A quarter circle with a right angle at its centre. The straight edge along the bottom is labelled ten centimetres, and the other straight edge is the same length.
What is the perimeter of the quarter circle in the last question, which has a radius of ten centimetres? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm.
A semicircle has a radius r. What is its perimeter?

A window is a rectangle with a semicircle on top. The rectangle part is one point four metres wide and one point two metres high. The semicircle has the one point four metres width as its diameter. What is the area of glass? Give your answer to two decimal places, in m squared. The picture shows: A window made of a rectangle, one point four metres wide and one point two metres tall, with a semicircle on top that has the same width.

A plastic pipe has an outer radius of three centimetres and an inner radius of two point five centimetres. What is the area of its cross-section (the plastic)? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm squared. The picture shows: A ring shape: a large circle with a smaller circle cut out of the middle. The outer radius is three centimetres and the inner radius is two point five centimetres.
A circular lawn has a radius of five metres. In the middle is a circular pond with a radius of one metre. How much grass is there? Give your answer to one decimal place, in m squared.
Key idea: when you work backwards from an area, you get r squared first. The last step is the square root. Then check by going forwards.
A circle has a circumference of thirty-two centimetres. What is its diameter? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm.
A tree trunk measures one hundred and forty centimetres round. Treat the trunk as a circle. What is its diameter? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm.
A circle has a circumference of forty-four centimetres. What is its radius? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm.
A wheel rolls two point one metres along the ground in one full turn. What is the diameter of the wheel? Give your answer to two decimal places, in m.
A circle has an area of one hundred and fifty-four centimetres squared. What is its radius? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm.
A circle has an area of two hundred centimetres squared. What is its radius? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm.
A circular pond has an area of twenty metres squared. What is its radius? Give your answer to one decimal place, in m.
The circumference of a circle is doubled. What happens to its diameter?
Key idea: find the fraction of the circle first, then multiply it by the full circumference (for the arc) or the full area (for the sector).
A sector has an angle of ninety degrees and a radius of eight centimetres. Work out its arc length. Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm.

What is the area of this sector? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm squared. The picture shows: A slice of a circle. The angle at the centre is one hundred and twenty degrees and the straight edges are each nine centimetres.
A sector has an angle of forty-five degrees and a radius of ten centimetres. Work out its arc length to one decimal place, in cm.
A sector has an angle of seventy-two degrees and a radius of five centimetres. Work out its area to one decimal place, in cm squared.
An arc has a length of ten centimetres and comes from a circle of radius twelve centimetres. What is the angle at the centre? Give your answer to one decimal place, in degrees.
Key idea: in terms of pi: work out the number part and write pi after it, like twenty-five pi. Square the radius, but do not square the pi.
