A cylinder has a radius of four centimetres and a height of ten centimetres. Work out its volume to one decimal place, in cm cubed.

A hot water tank is a cylinder with a diameter of zero point six metres and a height of one point two metres. one metre cubed is one thousand litres. How many litres does it hold? Give your answer to one decimal place.
A cylinder has a volume of five hundred centimetres cubed and a height of ten centimetres. What is its radius? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm.
A cylinder has a radius of three centimetres and a height of five centimetres. Its volume is ___ pi cm cubed. Type the number that goes in front of the pi.

A fencer needs to put edging round the outside of a round pond. What does she need to work out?

A round table top has a diameter of one point two metres. A carpenter fits a wooden strip right round the edge. The strip costs eight pounds fifty per metre. How much does the strip cost? Give your answer to two decimal places, like twelve point five zero.

This shape is a rectangle with a semicircle joined to one end. The rectangle is ten centimetres long and six centimetres wide. The diameter of the semicircle is the six centimetre side. A piece of string forty centimetres long makes the outline of a square with sides of ten centimetres. The string is then reshaped into a circle. What is the area of the circle? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm squared. Is it bigger than the area of the square?
The radius of a circle is doubled. How many times bigger is the new area? (Try it with a radius of three centimetres, then of five centimetres. Does the answer change?)

A rope is pulled tight round a circle (a ball, or the Earth). The rope is then made exactly one metre longer, and held at the same height above the circle all the way round. How far is the rope above the surface? Give your answer to two decimal places, in m. (The answer is the same for any size of circle.)

A plumber uses a hole saw to cut a round hole for a one hundred and ten millimetres waste pipe. The hole has a diameter of one hundred and ten millimetres. What is the area of the hole? Give your answer to one decimal place, in mm squared.

An electrician winds a cable round the core of a drum sixty times. The core has a diameter of twenty-five centimetres. Ignore the thickness of the cable. How many metres of cable are on the drum? Give your answer to one decimal place.

A carpenter cuts a round table top with a diameter of one point five metres. The board costs forty-two pounds per m squared. How much does the board for the table top cost? Use the full calculator value until the end, then give your answer to two decimal places, like twelve point five zero.

A copper pipe has an outer diameter of twenty-two millimetres. Its inner diameter is twenty point two millimetres. What is the area of the cross-section of the copper? Give your answer to one decimal place, in mm squared.

A builder pours a round concrete base for a hot tub. The base is a cylinder with a diameter of two point four metres and a depth of zero point one five metres. Key idea: the number of marks tells you how much to write. One mark is a short answer. Three or four marks need working. Always show your working when there are two or more marks.

Units and typing Speed: km/h, m/s or mph. Density: g/cm cubed or kg/m cubed. Pressure: N/m squared (newtons per square metre). Power: W or kW. Energy: J or kWh. Where a question gives the units, type the number only. Use a decimal for part of an hour: thirty minutes is zero point five hours. Money answers have two decimal places, like twelve point five zero. Type a rule such as d equals s times t as s*t, and a fraction rule such as d/s.
A car travels sixty miles in two hours at a steady rate. How many miles does it travel in one hour?
Make t the subject of d equals s times t. Type your answer like m/k.
Change two point five hours into minutes.
three books cost twelve pounds. How much do five books cost at the same price? Give your answer in pounds, like twelve point five zero.

Key idea: the units must match. If the speed is in km/h, the time must be in hours. Change minutes to hours by dividing by sixty: thirty minutes equals zero point five h, fifteen minutes equals zero point two five h, forty-five minutes equals zero point seven five h.
A car travels one hundred and eighty miles in four hours. What is its average speed in mph?
A runner goes at twelve metres/s for five seconds. How far does she go? Answer in metres.
Which formula for time is correct?

Use the triangle. A coach travels ninety kilometres at forty-five kilometres/h. How many hours does it take? The picture shows: A distance, speed and time triangle. The top part says D equals ninety kilometres. The bottom left says S equals forty-five kilometres per hour. The bottom right has a question mark for T.
A train travels at seventy-five mph for three hours. How far does it travel? Answer in miles.
A cyclist rides thirty-six kilometres in one hour thirty minutes. What is her average speed in km/h?
A delivery van drives forty-five miles at sixty mph. How many minutes does the drive take?
Key idea: do NOT find the mean of the two speeds. The time spent at each speed is different, so work out the total distance and the total time first. Include any stops in the total time.
A walker goes six kilometres in three hours, then four kilometres in one more hour. What is her average speed for the whole walk? Answer in km/h.
A driver covers one hundred miles in two hours, then one hundred and fifty miles in three hours. What is the average speed for the whole journey? Answer in mph.
A bus goes thirty miles at twenty mph, then thirty miles at thirty mph. What is its average speed for the whole journey? Answer in mph.
How do you find the average speed of a whole journey?

A driver sets off at zero nine:fifteen and arrives at eleven:forty-five. The journey is one hundred and fifty miles, including a thirty-minute rest. What is the average speed for the whole journey? Answer in mph.
Key idea: speed equals distance divided by time is the gradient. To find a speed, pick the two ends of a straight section: the change in distance divided by the change in time.

The graph shows a journey. What is the speed in the first hour? Answer in km/h. The picture shows: A graph with time in hours along the bottom and distance in kilometres up the side. A line goes up gently, then runs flat, then goes up steeply to its highest point, then comes back down to the bottom axis.

On the same graph, for how many hours was the traveller stopped? Answer in hours. The picture shows: A graph with time in hours along the bottom and distance in kilometres up the side. A line goes up gently, then runs flat, then goes up steeply to its highest point, then comes back down to the bottom axis.

On the same graph, what was the speed on the last section, when the traveller came back? Give the speed as a positive number, in km/h. The picture shows: A graph with time in hours along the bottom and distance in kilometres up the side. A line goes up gently, then runs flat, then goes up steeply to its highest point, then comes back down to the bottom axis.

On the same graph, how far did the traveller go altogether, there and back? Answer in km. The picture shows: A graph with time in hours along the bottom and distance in kilometres up the side. A line goes up gently, then runs flat, then goes up steeply to its highest point, then comes back down to the bottom axis.

On the same graph, what was the average speed for the whole journey from zero to four hours? Answer in km/h. The picture shows: A graph with time in hours along the bottom and distance in kilometres up the side. A line goes up gently, then runs flat, then goes up steeply to its highest point, then comes back down to the bottom axis.
On a distance-time graph, which part shows the fastest travel?
Key idea: km/h to m/s: divide by three point six. metres/s to km/h: multiply by three point six. A quick check: the same speed is a smaller number in m/s than in km/h.
Change thirty-six kilometres/h into m/s.

To change a speed from km/h to m/s, what do you do?
Key idea: water has a density of one gram/cm cubed. Anything with a density less than one gram/cm cubed floats in water. Anything with a density more than one gram/cm cubed sinks.
A block of metal has a mass of five hundred and forty grams and a volume of two hundred centimetres cubed. What is its density? Answer in g/cm cubed.
A metal has a density of eight grams/cm cubed. What is the mass of twenty-five centimetres cubed of it? Answer in grams.
A liquid has a density of zero point nine grams/cm cubed. It has a mass of seven hundred and twenty grams. What is its volume? Answer in cm cubed.
A piece of wood has a mass of one hundred and fifty grams and a volume of two hundred centimetres cubed. Water has a density of one gram/cm cubed. What happens in water?
A tub ten centimetres long, five centimetres wide and four centimetres high is filled with sand of mass three hundred grams. What is the density of the sand? Answer in g/cm cubed.
A steel plate has a volume of four hundred centimetres cubed and a density of seven point eight grams/cm cubed. What is its mass in kilograms, like two point seven five?

Key idea: to compare prices, work out the unit price of each (the price for one metre, one kilogram or one item), then compare. The lower unit price is the better buy.

A runner goes at four metres/s. How long does she take to run one point two kilometres? Answer in seconds.

A table pushes down with a force of six hundred N. The pressure on the floor is two thousand, four hundred N/m squared. What is the area of the table legs in contact with the floor? Answer in m squared.
Dan says: a bus goes thirty miles at thirty mph, then thirty miles at sixty mph. The average speed is (thirty plus sixty) divided by two equals forty-five mph. What went wrong?
Eve says: a trip of ten kilometres takes twenty minutes, so the speed is ten divided by twenty equals zero point five kilometres/h. What went wrong?
Ida says: a force of six hundred N acts on an area of three metres squared, so the pressure is six hundred times three equals one thousand, eight hundred N/m squared. What went wrong?
Which quantity is measured in N/m squared?
A car travels one hundred and fifty miles in two point five hours. What is its average speed in mph?
A block of copper has a mass of four thousand, four hundred and eighty grams and a volume of five hundred centimetres cubed. What is its density? Answer in g/cm cubed.
A force of three hundred and sixty N acts on an area of zero point one two metres squared. What is the pressure? Answer in N/m squared.
Cable costs one pounds thirty-five per metre. How much does eighteen metres cost? Give your answer in pounds, like twelve point five zero.
A one point five kW kettle runs for twenty minutes. How many kWh does it use?
A pump moves water at thirty-six litres per minute. How long does it take to empty a four hundred and fifty-litre tank? Answer in minutes.
A nine kW electric shower is used for ten minutes. How many kWh of energy does it use?
An oak plank measures two hundred centimetres by twenty centimetres by four centimetres and has a mass of twelve kilograms. What is the density of the oak? Answer in g/cm cubed.

A concrete slab is two metres long, one point five metres wide and zero point one metres thick. Concrete has a density of two thousand, four hundred kilograms/m cubed. What is the mass of the slab? Answer in kg.
A delivery van leaves at zero eight:fifteen and arrives at zero nine:forty-five after driving eighty-one miles without stopping. What is its average speed in mph?
An electrician is paid twenty-four pounds fifty an hour. How much does she earn for a job that takes six point five hours? Give your answer in pounds, like one hundred and twenty point five zero.

In a hydraulic jack, a force of four hundred and fifty N acts on a small piston of area zero point zero zero three metres squared. The same pressure acts on a large piston of area zero point zero two metres squared. What force acts on the large piston? Answer in N.
A cyclist rides eighteen kilometres in forty-five minutes, then twelve kilometres in fifteen minutes. Work out her average speed for the whole ride. Answer in km/h.

An aluminium bar is a cuboid measuring fifteen centimetres by four centimetres by three centimetres. The density of aluminium is two point seven grams/cm cubed. Work out the mass of the bar. Answer in grams.

A car drives ninety kilometres at sixty kilometres/h. It then drives the same ninety kilometres back at forty-five kilometres/h. Show that its average speed for the whole journey is fifty-one point four kilometres/h to one decimal place.

A water tank rests on four feet. Each foot has an area of twenty-five centimetres squared. The tank pushes down on the ground with a force of eight hundred N. Work out the pressure on the ground. Answer in N/cm squared.
A three kW heater runs for two hours thirty minutes. Electricity costs twenty-eight p per kWh. Work out the cost. Give your answer in pounds, like four point five zero.
A bar has a volume of zero point zero zero two metres cubed. It is made of a metal with a density of seven point eight grams/cm cubed. Work out the mass of the bar. Answer in kg.
A driver goes up a hill one mile long at thirty mph. How fast must she drive down the same mile to average sixty mph over the whole two miles?
Show that a speed of one metre/s is the same as three point six kilometres/h.

Block eigh has a volume of six hundred centimetres cubed and a density of two grams/cm cubed. Block B has a volume of four hundred centimetres cubed and a density of seven grams/cm cubed. They are stuck together. What is the density of the combined block? Answer in g/cm cubed.

Reading the probability of B | eigh The bar | is read given. the probability of B | eigh means the probability of B, given that eigh has happened. The event after the bar is the one you already know. It is the denominator of the fraction. the probability of eigh and B means both happen. the probability of eigh | B and the probability of B | eigh are usually not the same.
Work out one minus the fraction two over five,. Give your answer as a fraction, like three over eight.
Work out the fraction three over eight, times the fraction two over seven,, in its simplest form. Type it like three over ten.
The probability that a train is late is zero point six five. What is the probability that it is not late?
A fair coin is tossed and a fair dice is rolled. What is the probability of heads and a six? Type it like one over twenty.
Key idea: the probability of B | eigh equals the number who are both eigh and B divided by the number who are eigh. The given group, counted in full, is the denominator of the fraction.
One student is chosen at random from the class of sixty. What is the probability that the student is a girl? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over five.
One girl is chosen at random from the class. What is the probability that she walks to school? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over five.
One of the students who walk is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student is a girl? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over five.
One boy is chosen at random from the class. What is the probability that he takes the bus? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over five.
One of the students who take the bus is chosen at random. Which fraction gives the probability that the student is a boy, written the probability of boy | bus?

A heating firm made fifty call-outs. thirty were for gas boilers and six of those needed a new part. twenty were for oil boilers and eight of those needed a new part. One oil-boiler call-out is chosen at random. What is the probability it needed a new part? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over five.

Key idea: along a path, multiply the first branch by the second branch, where the second branch is the probability given the first. For and then without replacement, the denominator of the second fraction is one smaller.

A bag has five red and three blue counters. Two counters are taken at random without replacement. What is the missing probability on the tree, the chance the second counter is red when the first was red? Give your answer as a fraction, like three over eight. The picture shows: A tree diagram for two counters taken without replacement from a bag with five red (R) and three blue (B). The first branches are R with five over eight and B with three over eight. After a red, the second branches are R and B. After a blue, the second branches are R with five over seven and B with two over seven. One probability is missing and marked with a question mark.

Use the tree. What is the probability that both counters are red? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten. The picture shows: A tree diagram for two counters taken without replacement from a bag with five red and three blue. First branches: R five over eight and B three over eight. After a red: R four over seven and B three over seven. After a blue: R five over seven and B two over seven.

A box holds ten fuses and three of them are faulty. Two fuses are taken at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are faulty? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

The same box of ten fuses has three faulty ones. Two fuses are taken at random without replacement. What is the probability that exactly one is faulty? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

the probability of eigh equals zero point six and the probability of B | eigh equals zero point five. Use the probability of eigh and B equals the probability of eigh times the probability of B | eigh to find the probability of eigh and B.

A bag has four red and three blue counters. One blue counter is taken out and not put back. What is the probability that the next counter is also blue? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over five.
On the tree, the second branches have seven as the denominator but the first branches have eight. Why?

Key idea: the probability of B | eigh equals the probability of eigh and B divided by the probability of eigh. It is the same as the overlap over the given group. The formula works with counts or with probabilities.

The Venn diagram shows thirty students and the sports they play. A student is chosen at random from those who play football. What is the probability that they also play tennis? Give your answer as a fraction, like three over ten. The picture shows: A Venn diagram of thirty students. The football circle has thirteen only in football. The overlap with the tennis circle has five. The tennis circle has seven only in tennis. Outside both circles there are five.

A student is chosen at random from those who play tennis. What is the probability that they also play football? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten. The picture shows: A Venn diagram of thirty students. The football circle has thirteen only in football. The overlap with the tennis circle has five. The tennis circle has seven only in tennis. Outside both circles there are five.

A student is chosen at random from all thirty. What is the probability that they play football and tennis? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten. The picture shows: A Venn diagram of thirty students. The football circle has thirteen only in football. The overlap with the tennis circle has five. The tennis circle has seven only in tennis. Outside both circles there are five.

A student is chosen at random from those who do not play tennis. What is the probability that they play football? Give your answer as a fraction, like three over ten. The picture shows: A Venn diagram of thirty students. The football circle has thirteen only in football. The overlap with the tennis circle has five. The tennis circle has seven only in tennis. Outside both circles there are five.

The Venn diagram shows the forty students in a school who are in the maths club, the science club, both or neither. One maths club member is chosen at random. What is the probability that they are also in the science club? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten. The picture shows: A Venn diagram of forty students. twelve are only in the maths club, twelve are in both clubs, eight are only in the science club and eight are in neither.

One science club member is chosen at random from the same Venn diagram. What is the probability that they are also in the maths club? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten. The picture shows: A Venn diagram of forty students. twelve are only in the maths club, twelve are in both clubs, eight are only in the science club and eight are in neither.
Which formula gives the probability of B | eigh, the chance of B given eigh?

Key idea: test for independence by comparing the probability of B | eigh with the probability of B. If they are equal, the events are independent and the probability of eigh and B equals the probability of eigh times the probability of B. If they differ, the events are dependent. Picks with replacement are independent. Picks without replacement are dependent.
One part made by Machine X is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is faulty? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.
One part made by Machine Y is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is faulty? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.
Are faulty and made by Machine X independent for these parts?
Are faulty and made on the day shift independent for these parts?
eigh and B are independent events with the probability of eigh equals zero point five and the probability of B equals zero point four. What is the probability of eigh and B?
A fair coin is tossed and a fair dice is rolled. Given that the dice shows a six, what is the probability that the coin shows heads? Give your answer as a fraction, like three over ten.
Counters are picked one after the other from a bag. Which statement is correct?

Key idea: the probability of flagged | faulty and the probability of faulty | flagged are different questions with different denominators. Use counts out of a round number, like one thousand, to see which group is the denominator.

A test flags faulty parts. It was tried on one thousand parts: twenty faulty and nine hundred and eighty good. Use the tree to find the total number of parts that were flagged. The picture shows: The same tree of one thousand parts. twenty are faulty and nine hundred and eighty are good. Of the twenty faulty parts, eighteen are flagged and two are not. Of the nine hundred and eighty good parts, forty-nine are flagged and nine hundred and thirty-one are not.

A faulty part is tested. What is the probability that it is flagged? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten. The picture shows: The same tree of one thousand parts. twenty are faulty and nine hundred and eighty are good. Of the twenty faulty parts, eighteen are flagged and two are not. Of the nine hundred and eighty good parts, forty-nine are flagged and nine hundred and thirty-one are not.

A part is flagged. What is the probability that it really is faulty? Give your answer as a fraction, like three over ten. The picture shows: The same tree of one thousand parts. twenty are faulty and nine hundred and eighty are good. Of the twenty faulty parts, eighteen are flagged and two are not. Of the nine hundred and eighty good parts, forty-nine are flagged and nine hundred and thirty-one are not.

the probability of flagged | faulty is the fraction nine over ten, but the probability of faulty | flagged is only about zero point two seven. Why is the second one so much lower? The picture shows: The same tree of one thousand parts. twenty are faulty and nine hundred and eighty are good. Of the twenty faulty parts, eighteen are flagged and two are not. Of the nine hundred and eighty good parts, forty-nine are flagged and nine hundred and thirty-one are not.

A flagged part is checked by hand. What is the probability that it turns out to be a good part? Give your answer as a fraction, like three over ten. The picture shows: The same tree of one thousand parts. twenty are faulty and nine hundred and eighty are good. Of the twenty faulty parts, eighteen are flagged and two are not. Of the nine hundred and eighty good parts, forty-nine are flagged and nine hundred and thirty-one are not.
Key idea: the same overlap, divided by different groups, gives different answers. Say out loud which event is given, and put its probability or count on the denominator.
the probability of eigh equals zero point three, the probability of B equals zero point six and the probability of eigh and B equals zero point one two. Find the probability of B | eigh.
the probability of eigh equals zero point three, the probability of B equals zero point six and the probability of eigh and B equals zero point one two. Find the probability of eigh | B.
the probability of eigh equals zero point five and the probability of B | eigh equals zero point four. Find the probability of eigh and B.
the probability of B | eigh equals zero point four and the probability of eigh and B equals zero point two. Find the probability of eigh.
In a class of girls and boys, the probability of walk | girl equals the fraction three over five, and there are thirty girls. How many girls walk to school?
A bag has six counters, some red and the rest blue. Two are taken without replacement and the probability of both red equals the fraction one over five,. How many red counters are in the bag?
Sam says: in the class table, the probability of boy | bus equals the fraction sixteen over sixty,, because there are sixty students. What went wrong?

Mia says: a bag has five red and three blue counters. Two counters are taken at random without replacement, so the probability of both red equals the fraction five over eight, times the fraction five over eight,. What went wrong?
Kit says: the test flags ninety percent of faulty parts, so if a part is flagged there is a ninety percent chance it is faulty. What went wrong?

A bag has six red and two blue counters. Two counters are taken at random without replacement. What is the probability that the first is red and the second is blue? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

eighty people were asked. fifty own a car, and thirty of the car owners are over forty. One car owner is chosen at random. What is the probability they are over forty? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

twelve plumbers do gas work, nine do oil work and four do both. A plumber who does gas work is chosen at random. What is the probability that they also do oil work? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.
the probability of eigh equals zero point five and the probability of eigh and B equals zero point one five. Find the probability of B | eigh.
A fair dice is rolled and a fair coin is tossed. What is the probability of a six and tails? Give your answer as a fraction, like three over ten.

An electrician's tray has twelve fuses: four are thirteen amp and eight are five amp. She takes two fuses at random, without putting the first back. What is the probability that both are thirteen amp? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

A plumber buys one hundred valves: sixty from supplier eigh and forty from supplier B. three of A's valves leak and four of B's valves leak. A valve from supplier B is picked at random. What is the probability that it leaks? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

A carpenter has twenty planks and six of them are warped. She takes two at random without replacement. What is the probability that neither is warped? Give your answer as a fraction, like three over ten.

A tester checks five hundred sockets. twenty-five are faulty. The tester flags twenty-four of the faulty sockets and thirty-eight of the four hundred and seventy-five good ones. One of the flagged sockets is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is really faulty? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

A pack of fifteen roof tiles has three cracked ones. Two tiles are taken at random without replacement, and the first is cracked. What is the probability that the second is cracked as well? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

sixty percent of deliveries to a site arrive before nine am. Of those, five percent are damaged. Of the deliveries that arrive later, ten percent are damaged. In a group of fifty people, twenty-eight play chess, twenty play draughts and eight play both. A person who plays chess is chosen at random. Work out the probability that they also play draughts. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

A box has four red cards and three green cards. Two cards are taken at random without replacement. Work out the probability that at least one is green. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.
Machine P made sixty parts and nine were faulty. Machine Q made forty parts and two were faulty. Show that faulty and made by machine P are not independent events.
the probability of eigh equals zero point four. the probability of B | eigh equals zero point five. the probability of B | not eigh equals zero point two. Work out the probability of B.
the probability of eigh and B equals zero point one eight and the probability of B equals zero point four five. Work out the probability of eigh | B.

A test is tried on one thousand parts. forty are faulty and nine hundred and sixty are good. The test flags thirty-six of the faulty parts and forty-eight of the good parts. A flagged part is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is faulty? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

A bag has five red and three blue counters. Two counters are taken at random without replacement. Without drawing a tree, you might guess that the second counter is less likely to be red than the first. Work out the probability that the second counter is red. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form, like three over ten.

Three cards are in a hat. One has red on both sides, one has white on both sides and one has red on one side and white on the other. A card is drawn and put down with one side showing. The side you see is red. What is the probability that the other side is red as well? Give your answer as a fraction, like three over ten.

Events eigh and B are such that the probability of B | eigh equals the probability of B. Show that the probability of eigh | B equals the probability of eigh. (This shows that if B does not depend on eigh, then eigh does not depend on B.) Assume the probability of B is not zero.

Drawing rules Use a sharp pencil. Keep your construction arcs and lines: they show your method, so never rub them out. Exams usually allow a small error, about two millimetres on a length and two degrees on an angle. Measure carefully and check each step. You cannot draw on this screen, so the questions here ask you to work out lengths and angles, put steps in order, or say which construction or region you can see. Do the real drawing on paper with your own equipment.
Two angles of a triangle are fifty degrees and sixty degrees. What is the third angle? Answer in degrees.
A circle has a radius of three point five centimetres. What is its diameter? Answer in cm.
Two angles on a straight line are one hundred and fifteen degrees and x. Find x. Answer in degrees.
What is the area of a quarter of a circle with a radius of four centimetres? Give your answer to one decimal place, in cm squared.
Key idea: before you read a protractor, say whether the angle is acute (less than ninety degrees) or obtuse (more than ninety degrees). If your reading does not match, you are on the wrong scale.

The zero line of this protractor is along the arm on the right. What angle does the slanting arm make with it? Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A semicircular protractor with the zero line on the right and a second arm slanting upwards from the centre. Not marked with a number.

This time the zero line is the arm on the LEFT. What angle does the slanting arm make with it? Answer in degrees. The picture shows: A semicircular protractor with two scales. One arm lies along the left of the baseline, and a second arm slants up and to the left from the centre.
Which tool do you use to draw an arc?

Key idea: three lengths only make a triangle if the two shorter sides add up to more than the longest side. If they do not, the two arcs never meet.
You know all three sides of a triangle (SSS). Which is the correct order?

You are drawing a triangle with sides seven centimetres, five centimetres and four centimetres. You have drawn the seven centimetre side AB. You draw the four centimetres arc from B. What radius do you set on the compasses for the other arc, from eigh?
Can you construct a triangle with sides of three centimetres, four centimetres and eight centimetres?
A triangle has sides of six centimetres and four centimetres with an angle of fifty degrees between them (SAS). Which two tools do you need most?
A triangle has a side of eight centimetres. The angles at the two ends of that side are forty-five degrees and sixty-five degrees. What is the angle at the third corner? Answer in degrees.

A triangle is drawn with sides of six centimetres and eight centimetres and a right angle between them. How long is the third side? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A triangle with a right angle at eigh. Side AB is six centimetres and side AC is eight centimetres. The third side is the long slanting side.

Key idea: the arcs must use the SAME radius, and it must be more than half of AB, or they will not cross.
AB is nine centimetres long. Its perpendicular bisector cuts AB at M. How long is AM? Answer in cm.
AB is eight centimetres. A student sets the compasses to three centimetres and draws arcs from eigh and from B. What happens?

Arcs of radius six centimetres are drawn from eigh and from B. They cross at X. How far is X from B? Answer in cm. The picture shows: A horizontal line AB, six centimetres long. An arc above the line and one below, from each end, cross at points above and below the line. Both arcs have the same radius.
X is on the perpendicular bisector of AB. X is six point five centimetres from eigh. How far is X from B? Answer in cm.

A plumber marks the point on a pipe run that is the same distance from two connectors eigh and B. eigh and B are three point six metres apart on a straight line. How far from eigh is the point? Answer in m.
An angle of eighty-four degrees is bisected. How big is each of the two new angles? Answer in degrees.
An angle has been bisected and each half is twenty-seven degrees. How big was the whole angle? Answer in degrees.
In the angle bisector construction, you first draw an arc with the compass point on the corner O that cuts both arms. Why?

Which is the correct order to bisect an angle? Steps: (P) arcs of the same radius from the two points where the first arc meets the arms; (Q) line from the corner through where the new arcs cross; (R) an arc across both arms with the point on the corner.

To drop a perpendicular from a point P to a line, what do you do first?

Key idea: start at one and test each whole number in order. Stop when the numbers you are testing meet the partners you have already found. Each factor goes with its partner, so factors are multiples seen from the other side: three is a factor of twelve, and twelve is a multiple of three.

Why the tests for three and nine work: ten leaves remainder one when you divide by nine, so one hundred and one thousand do too (ninety-nine and nine hundred and ninety-nine are multiples of nine). So a number is its digit sum plus a multiple of nine. For example four thousand, five hundred and sixty-three equals four times nine hundred and ninety-nine plus five times ninety-nine plus six times nine plus (four plus five plus six plus three). The first three parts divide by nine, so only the digit sum, eighteen, decides. Since three divides nine, the same test works for three.

Key idea: start at the right-hand column. When adding, if a column totals ten or more, carry one into the next column to the left. How to use it: terms are in alphabetical order. Entries marked Higher are for Higher tier only. Filter by strand (an area of maths, such as Algebra) to see one area, search for a word, or jump to a letter.

Acute angle. An angle that is less than ninety degrees. Example: thirty-five degrees and eighty-nine degrees are acute. Watch out: Exactly ninety degrees is a right angle, not acute. The picture shows: An acute angle, less than ninety degrees

Adjacent (side). In a right-angled triangle, the side next to the angle you are using that is not the hypotenuse. Example: For a ladder leaning against a wall, the ground is the adjacent side for the angle between the ladder and the ground. Watch out: Two sides touch the angle. One is the hypotenuse, so adjacent is the other one. Flip it: Naming the sides from an angle, and choosing the angle from the sides.

Algebraic fraction. A fraction with algebra (a letter) in the numerator, the denominator, or both. It follows the same rules as a number fraction. Examples: the fraction three over x,, the fraction two x over five, and the fraction x plus one over x minus two, are algebraic fractions. the fraction x plus one over x minus two, is only defined when x is not two, because the denominator cannot be zero. Watch out: You can only cancel a factor (something multiplied), never a term (something added). the fraction x plus five over x, does not simplify to five. Flip it: Simplifying by factorising, and combining over a common denominator.

Algebraic proof. Showing something is true for every number by using letters to stand for any number. A few examples are not a proof. Example: Sum of three consecutive integers: n plus (n plus one) plus (n plus two) equals three n plus three equals three(n plus one), always a multiple of three. Watch out: Checking one plus two plus three and four plus five plus six is evidence, not proof.

Alternate angles. Angles between two parallel lines, on opposite sides of the line that crosses them, forming a Z shape. Alternate angles are equal. Example: If one angle is seventy degrees, the alternate angle is also seventy degrees. Watch out: Alternate angles are equal only when the two lines are parallel. The picture shows: Two parallel lines crossed by a third line

Alternate segment theorem. The circle theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord is equal to the angle in the alternate segment (the segment on the other side of the chord). Examples: A tangent at eigh and a chord AB make an angle of fifty-two degrees. For any point C in the alternate segment, angle ACB equals fifty-two degrees. Flip it: An angle between a tangent and a chord that matches an angle at the circumference tells you to use this theorem.

Ambiguous case. When the sine rule is used to find an angle, there can be two answers, θ and one hundred and eighty degrees minus θ, because they have the same sine. Example: sin thirty degrees equals sin one hundred and fifty degrees equals zero point five.

Angle. A measure of turn between two lines that meet at a point. It is measured in degrees: a full turn is three hundred and sixty degrees. Example: A right angle is ninety degrees. A straight line is an angle of one hundred and eighty degrees. Watch out: The size of an angle does not depend on how long the lines are drawn. The picture shows: An angle is the turn between two lines

Angle at the centre. The circle theorem: the angle at the centre of a circle is twice the angle at the circumference when both are made from the same arc (the same two points on the circle). Example: If the angle at the circumference is thirty-five degrees, the angle at the centre is seventy degrees.

Angle bisector. The line that cuts an angle exactly in half. Every point on it is the same distance from the two arms of the angle. Examples: The bisector of a seventy degrees angle makes two angles of thirty-five degrees. A mitre joint at a one hundred and twenty degrees corner is cut along the bisector, so each board is cut at sixty degrees. Flip it: Points the same distance from two lines that meet at a corner lie on this line.

Angle in a semicircle. The circle theorem: an angle drawn from the two ends of a diameter to any point on the circle is ninety degrees. Example: A triangle with the diameter as one side and its third corner on the circle is right-angled. Flip it: Converse: a right angle on the circle means its chord is a diameter.

Angle of depression. The angle measured down from the horizontal when you look down at something. Example: From a cliff top you look down at a boat. The angle between the horizontal and your line of sight is the angle of depression. Watch out: It is measured from the horizontal, not from the cliff or the vertical. Flip it: The angle of depression from eigh down to B equals the angle of elevation from B up to eigh.

Angle of elevation. The angle measured up from the horizontal when you look up at something. Example: You stand thirty metres from a tower and look up at the top. The angle between the horizontal and your line of sight is the angle of elevation. Flip it: The angle of elevation from B up to eigh equals the angle of depression from eigh down to B.

Arc. Part of the circumference of a circle: a curved piece of the edge. Examples: A sector with angle ninety degrees and radius eight centimetres has an arc length of ¼ times two pi times eight equals twelve point six centimetres (to one d.p.).

Area. The amount of flat space inside a shape. It is measured in square units such as cm squared. Examples: A rectangle five centimetres by three centimetres has area five times three equals fifteen centimetres squared. A square with side seven centimetres has area seven squared equals forty-nine centimetres squared. Watch out: Do not mix it up with perimeter, the distance round the edge. Flip it: From side length to area: square it. From area to side length: square-root it. The picture shows: Area is the space inside a shape

Asymptote. A line that a curve gets closer and closer to but never touches. Example: The graph of y equals one/x gets close to the x-axis and the y-axis but never meets either. Watch out: An asymptote is not part of the curve. The curve only gets nearer to it. Flip it: If a graph has an asymptote at x equals zero, the formula for the graph cannot be worked out at x equals zero.

Average. One number that stands for a whole set of data. The mean, median and mode are the three averages. Example: Data: two, three, three, seven. Mean three point seven five, median three, mode three. Each is a different kind of average. Watch out: In maths there are three averages. In everyday speech average usually means the mean. Flip it: From an average and how many values there are, you can work backwards to a missing value.

Average speed. The total distance of a journey divided by the total time taken, including any stops. Examples: thirty miles at thirty mph then thirty miles at sixty mph: total sixty miles in one point five hours, so the average speed is forty mph. Watch out: It is not the mean of the speeds, unless the same time is spent at each one. Flip it: From the parts of a journey to the average, and from the average to a missing part.

Axis (axes). One of the two number lines on a graph. The x-axis goes across and the y-axis goes up. Example: On a cost graph, hours might go along the x-axis and pounds up the y-axis. Watch out: Axes is the plural of axis.

Back bearing. The bearing of the way back. It is one hundred and eighty degrees different from the bearing you travelled on. Examples: The bearing of B from eigh is zero six five degrees, so the bearing of eigh from B is zero six five degrees plus one hundred and eighty degrees equals two hundred and forty-five degrees. From two hundred and eighty-five degrees the back bearing is two hundred and eighty-five degrees minus one hundred and eighty degrees equals one hundred and five degrees. Watch out: Add one hundred and eighty degrees if the bearing is below one hundred and eighty degrees. Subtract one hundred and eighty degrees if it is one hundred and eighty degrees or more.

Base (of a power). The number that is multiplied by itself in a power. In five to the power three, the base is five and the index is three. Example: five cubed equals five times five times five equals one hundred and twenty-five. The base is five. Watch out: The laws of indices only combine powers that have the same base.

Bearing. A direction, given as an angle measured clockwise from north and written with three figures. Examples: East is zero nine zero degrees, south is one hundred and eighty degrees and west is two hundred and seventy degrees. forty-five degrees clockwise from north is written zero four five degrees. Watch out: Always start from north and turn clockwise. "The bearing of B from eigh" starts at eigh. Flip it: Finding a bearing from a diagram, and using a bearing to find where you end up.

Best buy. The deal that costs least for the same amount. Work out the price per unit (per one hundred grams, per litre, per item) for each and compare. Example: five hundred grams for one pounds sixty is thirty-two p per one hundred grams. seven hundred and fifty grams for two pounds twenty-five is thirty p per one hundred grams, so the seven hundred and fifty grams pack is the better buy. Watch out: A bigger pack is not always cheaper per unit. Always work it out. Flip it: Price per unit, and how much you get for a pound.

bid mass. The agreed order for working out a calculation: Brackets, Indices (powers), Division and Multiplication together, then Addition and Subtraction together. Some people call it bod mass or PEMDAS. Example: three plus four times two equals three plus eight equals eleven (multiply before adding). (three plus four) times two equals fourteen (brackets first). Watch out: D and M have the same priority, and so do eigh and S: work left to right. eight divided by two times four equals sixteen, not one. A fraction bar and a root sign act like brackets. Flip it: Building a calculation with brackets to hit a target, and unpicking it step by step.

Box plot. A diagram of five numbers: the smallest value, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and largest value. The box shows the middle half of the data. Example: For the five numbers four, seven, twelve, eighteen and twenty-three, the box runs from seven to eighteen with a line at twelve, and whiskers go to four and twenty-three. Watch out: The width of the box is the interquartile range, not the range. Flip it: From a box plot you can read the five numbers back, and work out the interquartile range and the range.

Calculate. A question word: use maths to find a number. A calculator is usually allowed, and you should still show your working. Example: Calculate fifteen percent of eighty. Answer: zero point one five times eighty equals twelve. Watch out: Check the instructions on the paper: some papers do not allow a calculator.

Cancel. Divide the numerator and the denominator of a fraction by the same factor. The value of the fraction does not change. Examples: the fraction six x over nine,: divide the numerator and denominator by three to get the fraction two x over three,. the fraction three(x plus two) over x plus two,: the bracket (x plus two) is in both the numerator and the denominator, so it cancels, leaving three. Watch out: Only cancel factors that multiply the whole numerator and the whole denominator. In the fraction x plus five over x, the x in the numerator is added, so it cannot be cancelled.

Carrying and borrowing. In written addition you carry a ten into the next column when a column adds to ten or more. In written subtraction you borrow a ten from the next column when you cannot subtract. Example: eight plus four equals twelve: write two, carry one to the tens column. Watch out: Borrowing here means taking a ten from the next column, not asking a friend.

Chord. A straight line joining two points on a circle. The longest chord is a diameter. Example: A string stretched between two points on a hoop. The picture shows: A chord joins two points on a circle

Circle. A round shape where every point on the edge is the same distance from the centre. Examples: A coin, a wheel and the top of a tin are circles. A circle with radius three centimetres has diameter six centimetres.

Circumference. The distance all the way round the edge of a circle. It is the perimeter of a circle. Examples: C equals pi times d, or C equals two times pi times r, where d is the diameter and r is the radius. A circle with diameter ten centimetres has circumference pi times ten equals thirty-one point four centimetres (to one d.p.). Watch out: The circumference is a bit more than three times the diameter. Do not confuse it with the area, which uses r squared. Flip it: From circumference to diameter: divide by pi.

Class midpoint. The value halfway between the two ends of a class in a grouped table. It is used as the value for everything in that class when estimating the mean. Example: The class ten is less than t is less than or equal to twenty has midpoint (ten plus twenty) divided by two equals fifteen. Watch out: Using midpoints gives only an estimate of the mean, not the exact mean. Flip it: Estimated mean equals sum of (frequency times midpoint) divided by sum of frequencies.

Co-interior angles. Angles between two parallel lines, on the same side of the line that crosses them, forming a C shape. Co-interior angles add up to one hundred and eighty degrees. Example: If one angle is seventy degrees, its co-interior angle is one hundred and eighty degrees minus seventy degrees equals one hundred and ten degrees. Watch out: They are not equal, unless both are ninety degrees: they add up to one hundred and eighty degrees. The picture shows: Two parallel lines crossed by a third line
Coefficient. The number multiplying a letter in a term. Example: In five x the coefficient is five. In minus three y it is minus three. In x it is one.

Column vector. Two numbers written one above the other in brackets. The top number is the move across, and the bottom number is the move up or down. Examples: A move of three right and two down is the column vector with three on top and minus two underneath. In text we type it as three comma minus two. Watch out: Across first, then up: the same order as coordinates.

Commission. Extra pay for a worker, worked out as a percentage of what they sell. Example: five percent commission on two thousand pounds of sales is zero point zero five times two thousand equals one hundred pounds.

Common denominator. A denominator that two or more fractions share. You need one before you can add or subtract fractions. Example: the fraction one over three, plus the fraction one over four,: use twelve as the common denominator. the fraction four over twelve, plus the fraction three over twelve, equals the fraction seven over twelve,. Watch out: You add the numerators only, not the denominators. the fraction one over three, plus the fraction one over four, is not the fraction two over seven,.

Common difference. The amount a linear sequence goes up or down by each time. It is also the number in front of n in the nth term. Example: twenty, seventeen, fourteen, eleven, has common difference minus three. Watch out: If the terms go down, the common difference is negative. Flip it: Given the common difference and the first term, write the sequence or its nth term.

Compass point. One of the named directions: north, east, south and west, and between them north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west. Examples: North-east is zero four five degrees, south-east is one hundred and thirty-five degrees, south-west is two hundred and twenty-five degrees and north-west is three hundred and fifteen degrees.

Completing the square. Rewriting x squared plus bx plus c as (x plus p) squared plus q. It shows the turning point of the graph straight away. Example: x squared minus six x plus eleven equals (x minus three) squared plus two, so the turning point is three comma two.

Composite function. One function followed by another. f of g of x means do g first, then f. Example: f of x equals x plus one and g of x equals two x. f of g of three equals f of six equals seven but g of f of three equals g of four equals eight. Watch out: Order matters: fg and gf are usually different. The function written nearest x goes first.

Composite number. A whole number bigger than one that is not prime. It has more than two factors. Example: twelve is composite (factors one, two, three, four, six, twelve). thirteen is prime. Watch out: one is neither prime nor composite.

Compound interest. Interest that is added to the account each year, so later interest is worked out on the interest as well. Example: one thousand pounds at five percent a year for three years: one thousand times one point zero five cubed equals one thousand, one hundred and fifty-seven pounds sixty-three (to the nearest penny). Watch out: Three years at five percent is not fifteen percent. You multiply by one point zero five three times. Flip it: To find the starting amount, divide the final amount by the multiplier raised to the power n, where n is the number of years.

Compound measure. A measure made by combining two other measures, written with per or a division. Speed, density and pressure are compound measures. Examples: Speed is distance divided by time, in km/h. Density is mass divided by volume, in g/cm cubed. Watch out: Change the units so they match before you calculate, for example minutes into hours. Flip it: Finding the rate from two measures, and using the rate to find one of them.

Compound shape. A shape made by joining simpler shapes, such as rectangles, triangles and semicircles. Examples: An L-shape split into two rectangles: add their areas. Or draw a big rectangle round the shape, and subtract the area of the missing corner.

Conditional probability. The probability of an event when you already know another event has happened. the probability of B | eigh is read the probability of B given eigh. The event you already know about is the denominator of the fraction. Example: In a class of thirty girls and thirty boys, eighteen girls walk to school. the probability of walk | girl equals the fraction eighteen over thirty, equals the fraction three over five,. Watch out: the probability of B | eigh and the probability of eigh | B are usually different. They have the same numerator but different denominators. Flip it: the probability of B | eigh equals the probability of eigh and B divided by the probability of eigh, so the probability of eigh and B equals the probability of eigh times the probability of B | eigh.

Congruent. Exactly the same shape and exactly the same size. One can be slid, turned or flipped to fit onto the other. Examples: Two identical floor tiles are congruent. Congruent shapes are similar shapes with a scale factor of one. Watch out: Similar shapes can be different sizes. Congruent shapes cannot. Flip it: Showing that two triangles are congruent using SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS.

Conjugate (of a surd expression). The same two terms with the sign in the middle swapped. Multiplying an expression by its conjugate removes the surds. Examples: The conjugate of three plus square root of five is three minus square root of five. (three plus square root of five)(three minus square root of five) equals nine minus five equals four, with no surd left. Watch out: Only swap the sign between the two terms. Do not change the sign of the surd itself. Flip it: Used to rationalise a denominator that has two terms, like the fraction one over one plus square root of two,.
Consecutive. Following one after another with no gaps. Example: Consecutive integers: n, n plus one, n plus two. Consecutive odd numbers: two n minus one, two n plus one, two n plus three.

Constant of proportionality. The fixed number, usually called k, that links two quantities that are in proportion. In direct proportion k equals y divided by x. In inverse proportion k equals x times y. Examples: If five metres of cable cost twelve pounds, then k equals twelve divided by five equals two point four, the cost of one metre. If six workers take eight days, then k equals six times eight equals forty-eight worker-days. Flip it: Finding k from one pair of values, and using k to find any other pair.

Construction. An accurate drawing made with only a ruler, a protractor and compasses. The construction arcs and lines are kept to show the method. Examples: Drawing a triangle from its three sides, with arcs from each end of the base. Drawing the bisector of an angle with equal arcs. Watch out: Never rub out the arcs. They show how you did it. Flip it: Describing the steps of a construction from the finished drawing.

Converse. The reverse of a statement: swap "if" and "then". The converse of a true statement is not always true, but for Pythagoras' theorem it is. Example: Theorem: if a triangle is right-angled, then eigh squared plus b squared equals c squared. Converse: if eigh squared plus b squared equals c squared, then the triangle is right-angled. Flip it: The theorem and its converse are the two directions of one fact.

Coordinates. A pair of numbers x comma y that says where a point is on a grid: x is how far along, y is how far up. Example: The point three comma two is three along and two up. The point minus four comma three is four to the left and three up. Watch out: The x-coordinate always comes first. Going left or down from the origin gives negative values. Flip it: From a point on the grid to its coordinates, and from coordinates to a point.

Correlation. The link between two sets of data on a scatter graph. Positive correlation: both go up together. Negative correlation: one goes up as the other goes down. No correlation: no pattern. Example: Age of a car and its value show negative correlation: older cars are worth less. Watch out: Correlation shows a link, not a cause.

Corresponding angles. Angles in the same position at each of the two crossing points when a line crosses two parallel lines, forming an F shape. Corresponding angles are equal. Example: If the top-right angle at one crossing is seventy degrees, the top-right angle at the other is also seventy degrees. Watch out: Corresponding angles are equal only when the two lines are parallel. The picture shows: Two parallel lines crossed by a third line

Corresponding sides. Sides in the same place in two similar shapes. Each pair has the same scale factor. Examples: The shortest side of one triangle and the shortest side of a similar triangle are corresponding sides. Watch out: Match shortest to shortest and longest to longest before you divide.

Cosine (cos). For an angle in a right-angled triangle, cosine is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse. Examples: If the adjacent side is four and the hypotenuse is five, cos x equals the fraction four over five,. cos sixty degrees equals zero point five. Watch out: Make sure your calculator is in degrees. In a right-angled triangle, cosine is never more than one. Flip it: Finding a side with cos, and finding the angle with cos to the power of minus one.

Cosine rule. For any triangle: eigh squared equals b squared plus c squared minus two bc cos eigh, where side a is opposite angle eigh. Use it when you know all three sides, or two sides and the angle between them. Example: The rule becomes Pythagoras' theorem when eigh equals ninety degrees, because cos ninety degrees equals zero.

Cross-section. The flat shape you see when you slice straight through a solid. In a prism it is the same all the way along. Examples: Cut a pipe straight across and the cross-section is a ring. Cut a triangular tent straight across and the cross-section is a triangle.

Cube number. The answer when a whole number is multiplied by itself twice, so three copies of the number are multiplied together. It is the volume of a cube whose side length is that whole number. Example: one, eight, twenty-seven, sixty-four, one hundred and twenty-five, four cubed equals four times four times four equals sixty-four. Watch out: A negative number cubed stays negative: (minus two) cubed equals minus eight. Flip it: Cubing and cube-rooting undo each other. The picture shows: A cube number is the volume of a cube: two times two times two is eight

Cube root. The number that, multiplied by itself twice, gives the number you started with. It is written with the sign ∛. Example: ∛one hundred and twenty-five equals five because five times five times five equals one hundred and twenty-five. Watch out: Unlike square roots, a negative number does have a cube root: ∛(minus eight) equals minus two. Flip it: The inverse of cubing.

Cubic. An expression or graph whose highest power of x is three. The simplest cubic graph, y equals x cubed, is an S-shape through the origin. Example: y equals x cubed goes through minus two comma minus eight, zero comma zero and two comma eight. Watch out: A negative number cubed stays negative: (minus two) cubed equals minus eight. Flip it: To undo cubing, take the cube root.

Cuboid. A solid with six rectangular faces, like a brick or a shoebox. Examples: A cuboid eight centimetres by five centimetres by three centimetres: volume eight times five times three equals one hundred and twenty centimetres cubed.

Cumulative frequency. A running total of the frequencies: how many values there are up to and including the end of each class. Example: Frequencies four, twelve, twenty-eight give cumulative frequencies four, sixteen, forty-four. Plot them at the upper class boundaries to draw the cumulative frequency curve. Watch out: Plot each point at the upper boundary of its class, not at the midpoint. Flip it: The frequency of a class is how much the cumulative frequency rises across it.

Cyclic quadrilateral. A four-sided shape with all four corners on a circle. Its opposite angles add up to one hundred and eighty degrees. Example: If one angle is one hundred and ten degrees, the opposite angle is seventy degrees.

Cylinder. A solid with two equal circular ends and a curved side, like a tin of beans. It is a prism with a circle for its cross-section. Examples: Volume equals pi times r squared times h, where r is the radius and h is the height. Radius four centimetres and height ten centimetres: volume equals pi times sixteen times ten equals five hundred and two point seven centimetres cubed (to one d.p.).

Decimal. A number written with a decimal point. The digits after the point are parts of one: tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. Example: three point two five equals three plus two tenths plus five hundredths. zero point seven means seven tenths, which is the fraction seven over ten,. Watch out: Compare decimals column by column from the left, not by length: zero point four is bigger than zero point three five. The picture shows: A decimal: digits after the point are tenths, hundredths, thousandths

Decimal place (d.p.). The position of a digit after the decimal point. "To one d.p." means one digit after the point. Example: eight point six zero two to one d.p. is eight point six. seven point two one one one to one d.p. is seven point two. three point nine five to one d.p. is four point zero. Watch out: Look only at the digit after the place you are rounding to: five or more rounds up, four or less rounds down. Keep the trailing zero (four point zero) when asked for one d.p.

Deduce. A question word: work out a new fact from a fact you are given or have already found. Say which fact you used. Example: You are told twenty-three times fourteen equals three hundred and twenty-two. Deduce two point three times fourteen. Write: two point three is twenty-three divided by ten, so the answer is three hundred and twenty-two divided by ten equals thirty-two point two. Watch out: Do not start again with a calculator: use the fact you were given.

Denominator. The bottom number of a fraction. It tells you how many equal parts the whole is cut into, and so how big each part is. Example: In the fraction three over eight, the denominator is eight: the whole is cut into eighths. Watch out: A bigger denominator means smaller parts: the fraction one over eight, is smaller than the fraction one over four,. You do not add the denominators when you add fractions. The picture shows: The denominator is the bottom number: how many equal parts make the whole

Density. How much mass there is in each unit of volume. Density equals mass divided by volume. Examples: five hundred and forty grams in two hundred centimetres cubed is a density of two point seven grams/cm cubed. Water has a density of one gram/cm cubed, so things that are less dense than water float in it. Watch out: Keep the units matching: g with cm cubed, or kg with m cubed. one gram/cm cubed equals one thousand kilograms/m cubed. Flip it: From mass and volume to density, and from density and volume to mass.

Dependent events. Events where knowing one has happened changes the chance of the other, so the probability of B | eigh is not the same as the probability of B. Example: Taking two counters from a bag without replacement: the first pick changes what is left, so the second pick depends on it. Watch out: Picking with replacement gives independent events. Picking without replacement gives dependent events. Flip it: To test, compare the probability of B | eigh with the probability of B. If they differ, the events are dependent.

Deposit. Part of the price paid at the start. You pay the rest later. Example: A four hundred pounds sofa with a twenty-five percent deposit: deposit equals zero point two five times four hundred equals one hundred pounds. You still owe three hundred pounds.

Depreciation. When something loses value over time. If it loses the same percentage of its value each year, this is compound depreciation. Example: A car worth ten pounds zero zero zero loses fifteen percent of its value each year. After three years its value is ten thousand times zero point eight five cubed equals six thousand, one hundred and forty-one pounds twenty-five. Flip it: Compound growth (such as interest) is the same idea with a multiplier bigger than one.

Describe. A question word: say in words what you see or what happens. Give the key facts, and numbers where they matter. Example: Describe the pattern in three, seven, eleven, fifteen. Write: the numbers go up by four each time. Watch out: For a transformation, a full description needs the type and the details: for a translation, say translation and give the vector.

Diagonal. A straight line joining two corners of a shape that are not next to each other. Examples: The diagonal of a nine centimetres by twelve centimetres rectangle is fifteen centimetres (using Pythagoras' theorem). The picture shows: A diagonal joins two opposite corners

Diameter. A straight line across a circle that passes through the centre. Its length is twice the radius. Example: Radius four centimetres, diameter eight centimetres. The picture shows: The diameter goes across the circle through the centre

Difference. The result of subtracting the smaller number from the larger: how far apart two numbers are. Example: The difference between eighty-three and one hundred and twenty-seven is one hundred and twenty-seven minus eighty-three equals forty-four. Watch out: The difference is always the bigger number minus the smaller number, so it is never negative. From minus three to four the difference is four minus (minus three) equals seven.

Difference of two squares. An expression with one square taken away from another, such as x squared minus forty-nine. It factorises into two brackets that are the same except for the sign. Examples: x squared minus forty-nine equals (x plus seven)(x minus seven) seventy-three squared minus twenty-seven squared equals (seventy-three plus twenty-seven)(seventy-three minus twenty-seven) equals four thousand, six hundred Watch out: x squared plus forty-nine does not factorise this way. You need the minus sign. Flip it: Expanding (x plus eigh)(x minus eigh) gives x squared minus eigh squared: the two middle terms cancel.

Digit. One of the ten symbols zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine used to write numbers. Example: four thousand and eighty-two has four digits: four, zero, eight and two. The number fifty-two is made of the digits five and two. Watch out: A digit is a symbol; its value depends on where it sits (see place value).

Digit sum. The total you get by adding the digits of a number. It helps you test divisibility by three and by nine. Example: four thousand, five hundred and sixty-three has digit sum four plus five plus six plus three equals eighteen, so it is divisible by three and by nine.

Direct proportion. Two quantities are in direct proportion when one is always the same multiple of the other. When one doubles, so does the other. The rule is y equals kx, and the graph is a straight line through the origin. Examples: Cable costs three pounds per metre, so cost equals three times length. two metres costs six pounds, four metres costs twelve pounds, and zero metres costs zero pounds. Watch out: A straight line is not enough: it must pass through zero comma zero. A taxi fare with a start charge is not in direct proportion. Flip it: From the rule and one value to a missing value, and from two values back to the rule.

Discount. An amount taken off the normal price. Example: twenty percent off fifty pounds is a discount of zero point two times fifty equals ten pounds, so you pay forty pounds. Watch out: The discount is what is taken off. The sale price is what is left to pay.

Discriminant. The expression b squared minus four ac from the quadratic formula. Its sign tells you how many real solutions ax squared plus bx plus c equals zero has. Example: If the discriminant is positive, there are two solutions. If it is zero, there is one (repeated) solution. If it is negative, there are no real solutions, because you cannot take the square root of a negative number.

Distance-time graph. A graph with time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis. The gradient of a line is the speed, a flat line means the object has stopped, and a line going down means it is coming back. Examples: A line from zero comma zero to one comma thirty shows a speed of thirty kilometres/h. A flat line from one h to one point five h shows a thirty-minute stop. Watch out: The graph shows distance from the start, not the total distance travelled. Flip it: Reading a speed from the graph, and drawing a graph from a journey.
Dividend. The number that is being divided. Example: In eighty-four divided by seven equals twelve the dividend is eighty-four.

Divisible. A number is divisible by another if it divides into it exactly, with no remainder. Example: seventy-eight is divisible by six because seventy-eight divided by six equals thirteen. four thousand, five hundred and sixty-three is divisible by three because its digits add up to eighteen, which is a multiple of three. Watch out: Quick tests: a number is divisible by two if its last digit is even; by three if its digit sum is divisible by three; by nine if its digit sum is divisible by nine; by five if its last digit is zero or five; by ten if its last digit is zero. Flip it: If eigh is divisible by B, then B is a factor of eigh and eigh is a multiple of B.
Divisor. The number you divide by. Example: In eighty-four divided by seven equals twelve the divisor is seven. Watch out: A divisor is also a factor when it divides exactly.

Double inequality. An inequality with two signs, saying a value is between two numbers. Examples: minus two is less than x is less than or equal to three means x is bigger than minus two and at most three. A pipe cut to six hundred millimetres, with an error of up to two millimetres either way, has a length of x millimetres with five hundred and ninety-eight is less than or equal to x is less than or equal to six hundred and two. Watch out: Do the same step to all three parts when you solve one.

Elevation. The view of a three D shape from the front or from the side, drawn flat. There is a front elevation and a side elevation. Examples: The front elevation of a square-based pyramid is a triangle. The front elevation of a cylinder standing on its end is a rectangle. Flip it: Working out the solid from its plan and elevations.

Elimination. A way to solve simultaneous equations. Add or subtract the two equations so that one letter disappears, leaving one equation with one unknown. You may need to multiply an equation first so that the numbers in front of the letter match. Examples: x plus y equals seven and x minus y equals one. Add the equations: two x equals eight, so x equals four. Then four plus y equals seven, so y equals three. Watch out: If the letter you want to remove has the same sign in both equations, subtract. If the signs are different, add. Multiply every term of an equation, including the number on the right. Flip it: Check an answer by putting it back into both original equations.

Enlargement. A change of size where every length is multiplied by the same scale factor. The shape stays the same. Examples: A scale factor of three turns a four centimetre side into a twelve centimetre side. A scale factor less than one makes the shape smaller. Flip it: Finding the scale factor from two matching sides: new length divided by old length.

Equally likely. Outcomes that each have the same chance of happening, such as the faces of a fair dice. Example: A fair spinner with eight equal sectors: each sector has probability the fraction one over eight,. Watch out: Having three colours on a spinner does not make the probability of each colour the fraction one over three,. That only works if the sectors are the same size. Flip it: If outcomes are not equally likely, use relative frequency from an experiment instead.

Equation. Two expressions with an equals sign between them, saying they have the same value. Solving it means finding the value of the unknown that makes it true. Example: three x plus five equals twenty is true only when x equals five. Flip it: Solving finds the unknown from the equation; building an equation turns a puzzle into symbols.
Equidistant. The same distance from two or more things. Examples: The middle of a line is equidistant from its two ends. The centre of a circle is equidistant from every point on the circle.

Equivalent fractions. Fractions that look different but have the same value. Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number to make one. Example: the fraction one over two, equals the fraction two over four, equals the fraction three over six, equals the fraction fifty over one hundred,. Watch out: You must multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same number. Adding the same number to both changes the value. Flip it: Making a fraction with a bigger numerator and denominator (multiply both by the same number), and simplifying it (divide both by the same number).

Equivalent ratios. Ratios that describe the same split with different numbers. You get one by multiplying or dividing both numbers by the same number. Examples: two: three equals four: six equals ten: fifteen. Divide both numbers in twelve: eighteen by six to get the simplest form, two: three. Watch out: Adding the same number to both parts does not work: two: three is not the same as four: five. Flip it: Simplifying a ratio, and scaling it up.

Error interval. All the values a rounded number could really be, written as an inequality: lower bound is less than or equal to x is less than upper bound. Examples: seven to the nearest whole number: six point five is less than or equal to x is less than seven point five. two point four to one decimal place: two point three five is less than or equal to x is less than two point four five. Watch out: The lower bound is included (is less than or equal to) and the upper bound is not (is less than). Flip it: The number that was rounded is the middle of the interval.

Estimate. A sensible approximate answer, found by rounding the numbers to easy ones first. Example: forty-eight times twenty-one is about fifty times twenty equals one thousand. The exact answer is one thousand and eight. Flip it: Estimating is how you check an answer is the right size.

Evaluate. A question word: put numbers into an expression and work out its value. Example: Evaluate three eigh plus two when eigh equals four. Write three times four plus two equals fourteen. Watch out: In everyday English, evaluate can mean judge. In a maths exam it nearly always means work out the value.

Exact trig values. Exact values of sin, cos and tan for some angles, which you should know without a calculator. Example: sin thirty degrees equals the fraction one over two,, cos sixty degrees equals the fraction one over two,, tan forty-five degrees equals one, sin sixty degrees equals the fraction square root of three over two,.

Expand (multiply out). Remove brackets by multiplying every term inside by what is outside. With two brackets, multiply every term in one by every term in the other. Examples: three(x plus four) is identically equal to three x plus twelve (x plus two)(x plus five) is identically equal to x squared plus seven x plus ten Flip it: Factorising puts the brackets back.

Expected number. How many times you would expect something to happen on average: probability times the number of trials. Example: the probability of six equals the fraction one over six,. In one hundred and twenty rolls of a fair dice you expect the fraction one over six, times one hundred and twenty equals twenty sixes. Watch out: It is an average, not a promise. You will not get exactly twenty sixes every time. Flip it: Number of trials equals expected number divided by probability.

Explain. A question word: give a reason in words (and numbers) for why something is true. Example: Explain why one is not a prime number. Answer: it has only one factor, and a prime needs exactly two. Watch out: Write a full sentence that includes the word "because".

Exponential. A relationship where the unknown is in the power, like y equals two to the power of x. Each step of one along the x-axis multiplies y by the same number. Example: y equals two to the power of x gives one, two, four, eight, sixteen as x goes zero, one, two, three, four. Its graph crosses the y-axis at zero comma one. Watch out: two to the power of x is not two times x. A power means repeated multiplication. Flip it: To find the power that gives a number, ask how many times you must multiply: two to the power what is eight? The answer is three.
