Expression. Letters and numbers combined with operations, with no equals sign. You can simplify an expression but you cannot solve it. Example: three x plus five is an expression. three x plus five equals twenty is an equation. Watch out: In everyday English "expression" means a look on your face or a way of saying something. In maths an expression has no equals sign.

Exterior angle. An angle outside a shape at a corner, between one side and the next side extended in a straight line. Examples: A regular hexagon has exterior angles of three hundred and sixty degrees divided by six equals sixty degrees. The exterior angles of a polygon add up to three hundred and sixty degrees. Watch out: It is not the same as the interior angle. The two together make one hundred and eighty degrees. Flip it: Number of sides equals three hundred and sixty degrees divided by exterior angle (for a regular polygon). The picture shows: An exterior angle is outside the shape, between a side and the extended next side

Factor. A whole number that divides exactly into another number, with nothing left over. Example: The factors of twelve are one, two, three, four, six and twelve, because twelve divided by four equals three exactly. Flip it: Every factor has a partner: three times four equals twelve, so three and four are both factors of twelve. A multiple is the same fact seen from the other side.

Factor tree. A diagram that splits a number into smaller factors, branch by branch, until every branch ends in a prime number. Example: eighty-four splits into two and forty-two; forty-two splits into two and twenty-one; twenty-one splits into three and seven. The primes are two, two, three, seven.

Factorise. Write an expression as a product of factors, with brackets. It is expanding in reverse. Examples: six x plus nine is identically equal to three(two x plus three) x squared plus seven x plus ten is identically equal to (x plus two)(x plus five) Watch out: Check by expanding your answer: you should get the original back. Flip it: The reverse of expand.

Fibonacci-type sequence. A sequence where each term is the sum of the two terms before it. Example: one, one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, Another one starts four, five: four, five, nine, fourteen, twenty-three, Watch out: You need to be told the first two terms. Flip it: Going backwards, subtract: each term is the next one minus the one before.

Formula. A rule written with letters that links quantities. The plural is formulae. Example: Area of a rectangle: eigh equals l times w, where l is the length and w is the width. Perimeter of a rectangle: P equals two l plus two w.

Fraction. A number that describes equal parts of a whole. It is written with one number over another. Example: the fraction three over eight, means three of eight equal parts. three pieces of a pizza cut into eight equal slices. Watch out: The parts must be equal. A shape cut into three unequal pieces does not show thirds. The picture shows: A fraction shows parts of a whole

Frequency density. Frequency divided by class width. It is the height of a histogram bar. Example: Class twenty is less than l is less than or equal to fifty with frequency forty-five: class width thirty, so frequency density equals forty-five divided by thirty equals one point five. Watch out: Divide by the class width (upper boundary minus lower boundary), not by the boundary itself. Flip it: Frequency equals frequency density times class width.

Frequency table. A table that counts how many times each value occurs. The frequency (f) is the count. Example: Goals scored in a match: zero, one and two, with frequencies four, five and six. The mean number of goals is (zero times four plus one times five plus two times six) divided by fifteen equals seventeen divided by fifteen. Watch out: The mode is the value with the biggest frequency, not the frequency itself. Flip it: Mean equals sum of (frequency times value) divided by sum of frequencies.
Frustum. What is left of a cone or pyramid when the top is removed by a cut parallel to the base. Example: A lampshade or a flowerpot.
Function. A rule that turns each input into exactly one output. Example: f of x equals three x minus one means "multiply by three, then subtract one". f of four equals eleven.

Geometric sequence. A sequence where each term is the one before multiplied by the same number. Example: two, six, eighteen, fifty-four, multiplies by three each time. eighty, forty, twenty, ten, multiplies by the fraction one over two, each time. Watch out: The gaps are not equal. Divide neighbouring terms to find the multiplier. Flip it: Going back along the sequence means dividing by the multiplier.

Gradient. How steep a line is: rise divided by run. A line that goes up to the right has a positive gradient, and one that goes down has a negative gradient. Example: A line through one comma two and four comma eleven rises nine over a run of three, so its gradient is nine divided by three equals three. Watch out: It is rise divided by run, not run divided by rise. Check the sign against the picture. Flip it: Given the gradient and a point, you can draw or write the line.

Hence. A question word: use the result you found in the previous part to get the next answer. The question wants you to use your last result, not start again. Example: Factorise x squared plus five x plus six to get (x plus two)(x plus three). Hence solve x squared plus five x plus six equals zero. Use the brackets: x equals minus two or x equals minus three. Watch out: If you ignore the earlier part and use another method, you may lose the marks.

Highest common factor (HCF). The biggest number that is a factor of two or more numbers. Example: Factors of twelve: one, two, three, four, six, twelve. Factors of eighteen: one, two, three, six, nine, eighteen. The biggest in both lists is six, so HCF twelve comma eighteen equals six. Flip it: The HCF of the numerator and denominator is the number to divide both by, to simplify a fraction in one go: the fraction twelve over eighteen, equals the fraction two over three,.

Histogram. A graph of grouped data with touching bars. When the classes have different widths, the height of a bar is the frequency density and its area shows the frequency. Example: A bar from twenty to forty with height three point five has area three point five times twenty equals seventy, so the frequency is seventy. Watch out: A histogram is not a bar chart. With unequal widths, the height is not the frequency. Flip it: To draw one, divide each frequency by its class width. To read one, multiply each height by its width.

Hypotenuse. The longest side of a right-angled triangle. It is always opposite the right angle. Example: In a triangle with sides three, four and five, the hypotenuse is five. Watch out: Look for the right angle first, then pick the side opposite it. Do not pick it because it is "the slanted one". The picture shows: The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle

Identity (is identically equal to). Two expressions that are equal for every value of the letters. It is written with the symbol is identically equal to (three parallel lines), read as "is identically equal to" or "is equivalent to". An equation, written with equals, is only true for some values. Examples: two(x plus three) is identically equal to two x plus six is true whatever x is two x plus six equals ten is an equation: it is true only when x equals two Watch out: Expanding and factorising give identities. A single equals is often used in exam answers too, but is identically equal to shows you know the two sides are always the same. Flip it: Expanding and factorising are the two directions of one identity.

Image. The shape you get after a transformation. The shape you start with is called the object. Examples: Triangle ABC is reflected. The new triangle is the image, and its corners are labelled eigh′, B′ and C′.

Improper fraction. A fraction where the numerator is bigger than or equal to the denominator, so it is worth one or more. It is also called a top-heavy fraction. Example: the fraction seven over four, equals one the fraction three over four,. Flip it: Convert an improper fraction to a mixed number to see its size. Convert a mixed number to an improper fraction before multiplying or dividing.
Included angle. The angle between two given sides of a triangle. Example: The area formula the fraction one over two, ab sin C needs the included angle C between sides a and b.

Independent events. Events where one does not change the chance of the other. For independent events, the probability of eigh and B equals the probability of eigh times the probability of B. Example: Toss a coin and roll a dice: the probability of heads and six equals the fraction one over two, times the fraction one over six, equals the fraction one over twelve,. Watch out: Picking without replacement gives events that are not independent: the first pick changes what is left. Flip it: If the probability of eigh and B is not the probability of eigh times the probability of B, the events affect each other.

Inequality. A statement that one amount is bigger or smaller than another, using is less than, is greater than, is less than or equal to or is greater than or equal to, instead of saying they are equal. Examples: x is greater than two means x is any number bigger than two. x is less than or equal to five means x is five or smaller. A lift that carries at most eight hundred kilograms has a load of w kilograms, where w is less than or equal to eight hundred. Watch out: The line under is less than or equal to and is greater than or equal to means or equal to, so the number itself is allowed. Dividing both sides by a negative number turns the inequality sign round. Flip it: From the answer back to the inequality: put the boundary value in and check numbers either side.

Integer. A whole number. It can be positive, negative or zero. Example: Integers:, minus two, minus one, zero, one, two, Not integers: two point five, the fraction one over two,, minus zero point three. Watch out: Zero is an integer. A fraction such as the fraction six over three, is an integer too, because it equals two.

Interior angle. An angle inside a shape, at one of its corners. Examples: A triangle has three interior angles. They add up to one hundred and eighty degrees. The interior angles of a regular pentagon are each one hundred and eight degrees. Watch out: Interior means inside. The exterior angle at the same corner is outside. Flip it: At each corner: interior angle plus exterior angle equals one hundred and eighty degrees. The picture shows: An interior angle is inside the shape at a corner

Interquartile range. The upper quartile minus the lower quartile. It is the spread of the middle half of the data, so it ignores very high and very low values. Example: Lower quartile fourteen and upper quartile twenty-nine give an interquartile range of twenty-nine minus fourteen equals fifteen. Watch out: Subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile; do not add them. It is not the same as the range. Flip it: From the interquartile range and one quartile you can find the other quartile.

Interval. All the numbers between two given numbers. Examples: A solution between one point two and one point three lies in the interval from one point two to one point three. Flip it: Showing a solution lies in an interval by a change of sign, and shrinking the interval.

Inverse function. The function f to the power of minus one that undoes f. Example: f of x equals three x minus one: multiply by three, then subtract one. f inverse of x equals the fraction x plus one over three,: add one, then divide by three. Watch out: f inverse of x does not mean one over f of x. Flip it: Undo the steps in reverse order.

Inverse operation. The operation that undoes another. Adding undoes subtracting, and multiplying undoes dividing. Example: x plus seven equals twelve: the inverse of plus seven is minus seven, so x equals twelve minus seven equals five. Flip it: This is the heart of the book: every operation has a partner that undoes it.

Inverse proportion. Two quantities are in inverse proportion when one is halved as the other is doubled. Their product is always the same. The rule is y equals k divided by x, and the graph is a curve that falls and never touches the axes. Examples: six workers take eight days, so twelve workers take four days. With x workers and y days, x times y equals forty-eight every time, so y equals forty-eight divided by x. Watch out: More workers means fewer days. Do not multiply when you should divide. Flip it: From the rule to a missing value, and from two values back to k.

Inverse trig functions. Calculator buttons (sin to the power of minus one, cos to the power of minus one, tan to the power of minus one) that turn a ratio back into an angle. Example: sin x equals zero point five, so x equals sin to the power of minus one (zero point five) equals thirty degrees. Watch out: You usually press SHIFT or 2nd first. The sin to the power of minus one button is not one divided by sin. Flip it: Angle to ratio (sin), and ratio to angle (sin to the power of minus one).

Irrational number. A number that cannot be written as a fraction. Its decimal never ends and never repeats. Example: square root of two equals one point four one four two one, and pi are irrational. zero point three three three, is not irrational: it repeats, and equals the fraction one over three,. Watch out: A decimal that goes on for ever is not always irrational. Repeating decimals are fractions.

Isosceles triangle. A triangle with two equal sides. The angles opposite the equal sides are also equal. Example: Two radii of a circle and the chord between their ends make an isosceles triangle. The picture shows: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides

Iteration. Repeating a rule again and again, using each answer as the next input, to get closer and closer to a solution. Examples: xn plus one equals two xn plus one with x0 equals three gives seven, fifteen, thirty-one,, Use the Ans button on a calculator. Watch out: Keep every digit on the calculator and round only the final answer. Flip it: Repeating the rule forwards, and solving L equals f of L to find where the terms settle.

Iterative formula. A rule written xn plus one equals f of xn that gives the next term from the current one. Examples: xn plus one equals ∛(three minus xn) comes from x cubed plus x minus three equals zero. Watch out: Not every rearrangement gets closer to the solution. Some move further away from it. Flip it: Rearranging an equation into a formula, and finding the equation a formula solves.

Justify. A question word: give the reasons that show your answer or choice is right. Use numbers and a maths fact. Example: Is fifty-one a prime number? Justify your answer. Write: No, because three times seventeen equals fifty-one, so fifty-one has more than two factors. Watch out: Yes or no on its own gets no marks. The reason is what earns them.

Kilowatt-hour (kWh). A unit of energy: the energy used by a one kW appliance running for one hour. Energy in kWh equals power in kW times time in hours. Examples: A three kW heater running for four hours uses twelve kWh. At twenty-eight p per kWh, that costs twelve times twenty-eight equals three hundred and thirty-six p equals three pounds thirty-six. Watch out: A kWh is energy, not power. Change watts into kilowatts and minutes into hours first. Flip it: From power and time to energy and cost, and from energy and time back to power.

Laws of indices. Rules for powers of the same base: add the powers when multiplying, subtract the powers when dividing, and multiply the powers when raising a power to a power. A negative power means one divided by the positive power; a fractional power means a root. Example: a to the power of m times a to the power of n equals a to the power of m plus n; a to the power of minus n equals the fraction one over an,; nine to the power of one over two equals square root of nine equals three. Watch out: The laws for multiplying and dividing powers only work when the bases are the same.

Like terms. Terms that have exactly the same letter part, so they can be added or subtracted. Example: three a and five a are like terms: three eigh plus five eigh equals eight eigh. three a and three b are not, and neither are three a and three eigh squared. Watch out: Each term keeps the sign in front of it: in five x plus two minus x the x terms are five x and minus x. Flip it: Collecting like terms simplifies; the reverse is splitting a term up.

Line of best fit. A straight line drawn through the middle of the points on a scatter graph, with about as many points above it as below. Example: Draw it with a ruler. To estimate a y-value, go up from the x-value to the line, then across to the y-axis. Watch out: The line does not have to go through the origin. Estimates far outside the data (extrapolation) are unreliable. Flip it: You can read a y-value from an x-value, or an x-value from a y-value.

Line of symmetry. A line that cuts a shape into two halves that are mirror images of each other. Folding along the line makes the halves match. Examples: A rectangle has two lines of symmetry. A square has four. A regular hexagon has six.

Line of symmetry (of a parabola). The vertical line through the turning point of a parabola. The curve is a mirror image of itself on either side of it. Example: y equals x squared minus four x plus three has roots one and three, so its line of symmetry is x equals two, halfway between them. Watch out: It is a vertical line, so its equation is x equals a number, not y equals a number. Flip it: If you know the line of symmetry and one root, the other root is the same distance on the other side.

Linear sequence. A sequence that goes up or down by the same amount each time. Its nth term has the form an plus b. Example: four, seven, ten, thirteen, goes up by three, and its nth term is three n plus one. Watch out: If the gaps themselves change, it is not linear. Check the gaps first. Flip it: Find the nth term from the terms: the common difference is a, then use the first term to find b.

Locus (loci). The set of all the points that follow one rule. It can be a line, a curve or a whole region. The plural is loci. Examples: The locus of points exactly three centimetres from a point P is a circle with radius three centimetres. The locus of points the same distance from eigh and B is the perpendicular bisector of AB. Watch out: Exactly gives the line or curve. Less than gives the inside, and more than gives the outside. Flip it: Say the rule from a picture of the locus.

Loss. The amount of money lost when the costs are more than the money you receive. Example: You buy a bike for eighty pounds and sell it for seventy pounds. Loss equals eighty minus seventy equals ten pounds.

Lower bound. The smallest value a rounded or measured number could really be. For a rounded number it is the number minus half the rounding unit. Examples: A plank of length two point four metres, to one decimal place, has lower bound two point four minus zero point zero five equals two point three five metres. seven to the nearest whole number has lower bound six point five. Watch out: Use half the rounding unit, not the whole unit. Flip it: The rounded number is halfway between the lower and upper bounds.

Lowest common multiple (LCM). The smallest number that is a multiple of two or more numbers. Example: Multiples of four: four, eight, twelve, Multiples of six: six, twelve, The first in both is twelve, so LCM four comma six equals twelve. Flip it: The LCM of two denominators is the smallest common denominator, which makes adding fractions easiest.

Magnitude. The length of a vector. For the vector with x across and y up it is the square root of (x squared plus y squared), from Pythagoras. Examples: The vector five comma minus twelve has magnitude square root of (twenty-five plus one hundred and forty-four) equals square root of one hundred and sixty-nine equals thirteen. Watch out: Square the numbers first, then add. A magnitude is never negative.

Map scale. A ratio that compares a length on a map, plan or model with the real length. The same unit is used on both sides of the ratio. Example: A scale of one: fifty thousand means one centimetre on the map is fifty thousand centimetres (five hundred metres) in real life. Watch out: Change units at the end: multiply by the scale, then change centimetres to metres or kilometres. Flip it: Map length to real length, and real length to map length.

Mean. The average found by adding all the values and dividing by how many there are. Example: Mean of two, three, seven: (two plus three plus seven) divided by three equals four. Watch out: In everyday English "mean" can mean unkind or "to signify". In maths it is the "fair share" average. Flip it: From a mean and a count you can find the total: total equals mean times number of values.

Median. The middle value when the data are in order from smallest to largest. With two middle values, take the number halfway between them. Example: two, three, seven, eight, twenty: the median is seven. For two, three, seven, eight the median is five.

Metric prefix. A short word or letter in front of a unit that stands for a power of ten, such as kilo (k), mega (M) and milli (m). Examples: kilo (k) equals ten cubed, so one kW equals one thousand W milli (m) equals ten to the power of minus three, so one mA equals zero point zero zero one eigh Flip it: To change to a bigger unit, divide by the power of ten. To change to a smaller unit, multiply by it.

Midpoint. The point exactly halfway along a line segment. Add the x-coordinates and halve, and do the same for y. Example: The midpoint of two comma four and eight comma ten is ((two plus eight) divided by two, (four plus ten) divided by two) equals five comma seven. Watch out: Halve the totals of the coordinates. Do not give the gap between the points. Flip it: Given the midpoint and one end, go the same step again to find the other end.

Mixed number. A whole number and a fraction written together. Example: two the fraction one over three, means two plus the fraction one over three,. As an improper fraction: two the fraction one over three, equals the fraction seven over three,. Watch out: To multiply or divide, convert to an improper fraction first: two the fraction one over three, times three equals the fraction seven over three, times three equals seven. Do not treat the whole number and the fraction separately.

Modal class. In a grouped table, the class with the biggest frequency. Example: If the class ten is less than t is less than or equal to twenty has the biggest frequency, it is the modal class. Watch out: Give the class, not the frequency.
Mode. The value that occurs most often. Example: two, three, three, seven: the mode is three.

Multiple. A number in the times table of another number: what you get by multiplying that number by a whole number. Example: Multiples of six: six, twelve, eighteen, twenty-four, thirty, Flip it: eighteen is a multiple of six and six is a factor of eighteen: one fact, two views.

Multiplier. A single number you multiply a quantity by to make a percentage change in one step. Example: A fifteen percent decrease has multiplier zero point eight five. A seven percent increase has multiplier one point zero seven. Flip it: To undo a percentage change, divide by the same multiplier.

Mutually exclusive. Outcomes that cannot happen at the same time. For mutually exclusive outcomes, the probability of eigh or B equals the probability of eigh plus the probability of B. Example: On one roll of a dice, a two and a five are mutually exclusive, so the probability of two or five equals the fraction one over six, plus the fraction one over six, equals the fraction one over three,. Watch out: On one roll of a dice, even and bigger than three can both be true (four and six), so adding their probabilities would count four and six twice. Flip it: If the probability of eigh or B is not the probability of eigh plus the probability of B, the outcomes overlap.

Negative number. A number below zero, written with a minus sign. On a number line it is to the left of zero. Example: Temperature drops from three degrees Celsius to minus four degrees Celsius: a fall of seven degrees. three minus seven equals minus four. Watch out: Subtracting a negative adds: five minus (minus two) equals seven. The picture shows: Negative numbers are to the left of zero

nth term. A formula that gives any term of a sequence from its position n. Example: For three, seven, eleven, fifteen, the nth term is four n minus one. The 10th term is four times ten minus one equals thirty-nine.

Number line. A straight line with numbers marked at equal spacing, increasing from left to right. It continues on the left of zero for negative numbers. Example: On a number line minus two is to the right of minus ten, so minus two is the bigger number. The picture shows: A number line with negative and positive numbers

Numerator. The top number of a fraction. It counts how many parts you have. Example: In the fraction three over eight, the numerator is three: three parts. Watch out: Memory hook: the numerator tells you the number of parts, and it sits at the top. The picture shows: The numerator is the top number: how many parts you have

Obtuse angle. An angle that is more than ninety degrees and less than one hundred and eighty degrees. Example: one hundred and twenty degrees and one hundred and seventy-nine degrees are obtuse. The picture shows: An obtuse angle, between ninety and one hundred and eighty degrees

Operation. A mathematical process such as add, subtract, multiply or divide. Squaring and square-rooting are operations too. Example: The four operations: plus, minus, times, divided by. Flip it: Every operation has an inverse that undoes it.

Opposite (side). In a right-angled triangle, the side across from the angle you are using. It does not touch that angle. Example: If the angle is at the bottom right of a triangle with its right angle at the bottom left, the opposite side is the upright one. Watch out: It changes if you pick the other angle. The hypotenuse never changes. Flip it: Naming the sides from an angle, and choosing the angle from the sides.
Origin. The point zero comma zero where the x-axis and the y-axis cross. Example: The point zero comma five is five units above the origin.

Outcome. One possible result of an experiment or event, such as getting heads when you toss a coin. Example: Rolling a dice has six outcomes: one, two, three, four, five and six. Tossing two coins has four outcomes: HH, HT, TH and TT. Watch out: HT and TH are different outcomes. List them both. Flip it: If you know how many outcomes there are and how many are favourable, you can work out the probability.

Outlier. A value that is far away from the rest of the data. It can drag the mean a long way. Example: Pay in pounds: twenty-four thousand, twenty-five thousand, twenty-six thousand, twenty-seven thousand, ninety-eight thousand. The ninety-eight thousand is an outlier. Watch out: The median is hardly changed by an outlier, but the mean and the range are. Flip it: To describe typical data with an outlier, use the median instead of the mean.

Parabola. The U-shaped curve that is the graph of a quadratic. If the x squared term is negative, it is an upside-down U. Example: y equals x squared minus x minus six is a parabola that crosses the x-axis at x equals minus two and x equals three.

Parallel. Straight lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet. They are marked with matching arrows. Example: The two long edges of a rectangle are parallel. Watch out: Two straight lines that cross each other are not parallel. The picture shows: Parallel lines never meet

Parallelogram. A four-sided shape with two pairs of parallel sides. Opposite sides are equal in length. Examples: Base nine centimetres and perpendicular height four centimetres: area equals nine times four equals thirty-six centimetres squared. Flip it: From area to base: divide the area by the perpendicular height.

Partitioning. Splitting a number into easy parts so you can calculate in steps. Example: thirty-six times twenty-four equals thirty-six times twenty plus thirty-six times four equals seven hundred and twenty plus one hundred and forty-four equals eight hundred and sixty-four.

Pence. A unit of UK money. There are one hundred pence (one hundred p) in one pounds. Example: sixty-five p equals sixty-five pence. two pounds forty equals two hundred and forty p. Watch out: Put the answer in the unit the question asks for. Do not write sixty-five pencep, which mixes the two.

Percentage. A fraction out of one hundred. The symbol percent means "per hundred". Example: thirty-five percent equals the fraction thirty-five over one hundred, equals zero point three five. thirty-five percent of eighty equals zero point three five times eighty equals twenty-eight. Flip it: Writing a fraction as a percentage and a percentage as a fraction.

Percentage change. How much an amount has changed, written as a percentage of the starting amount: change divided by original, times one hundred. Example: A price goes from eighty pounds to ninety-two pounds. The change is twelve pounds. twelve divided by eighty times one hundred equals fifteen percent, so it is a fifteen percent increase. Watch out: Always divide by the original amount, not the new one. Flip it: To go from a percentage change to the new amount, use a multiplier.

Percentile. A value that a given percentage of the data lies below. The 90th percentile has ninety percent of the values below it. Example: For one hundred cable lengths, find ninety on the cumulative frequency (vertical) axis, read across to the curve, then down to the horizontal axis to find the 90th percentile. Flip it: From a value on the horizontal axis, go up to the curve and then across to the vertical axis to find what percentage of the data is below it.

Perimeter. The distance all the way round the edge of a shape. Examples: A rectangle five centimetres by three centimetres has perimeter five plus three plus five plus three equals sixteen centimetres. Watch out: Perimeter is a length (cm, m). Area is the space inside (cm squared, m squared). The picture shows: The perimeter is the distance all the way round

Perpendicular. At right angles to each other (ninety degrees). Two lines that are neither horizontal nor vertical are perpendicular if their gradients multiply to minus one. Example: Gradients two and minus the fraction one over two, give two times (minus the fraction one over two,) equals minus one, so those lines are perpendicular.

Perpendicular bisector. The line that cuts another line exactly in half, at a right angle. Every point on it is the same distance from the two ends. Examples: The perpendicular bisector of a line AB eight centimetres long meets AB four centimetres from eigh. Any point on it is the same distance from eigh and from B. Flip it: Points the same distance from two points eigh and B lie on this line.

Perpendicular height. The height of a shape measured at a right angle to its base. It is not the length of a slanting side. Examples: A triangle has a base of ten centimetres, slanting sides of thirteen centimetres and a perpendicular height of twelve centimetres. Its area is ½ times ten times twelve equals sixty centimetres squared. The thirteen centimetres is not used. Watch out: The slanting side is always longer than the perpendicular height. Use the one at a right angle to the base.

Pi (pi). The number you get when you divide the circumference of any circle by its diameter. It is about three point one four one five nine, and its decimal digits never end or repeat. Examples: Circumference equals pi times diameter. Area equals pi times radius squared. Use the pi button on your calculator. Only use three point one four if the question says so. Watch out: Do not round pi early. Keep the full value on the calculator and round the final answer.

Pie chart. A circle cut into sectors, where the angle of each sector shows its share of the whole. The angles add up to three hundred and sixty degrees. Example: forty children, fifteen chose cats. One child is shown by three hundred and sixty divided by forty equals nine degrees, so cats get fifteen times nine equals one hundred and thirty-five degrees. Watch out: A pie chart with no total cannot be used to compare numbers between two charts. Flip it: To read a pie chart backwards, divide an angle by the degrees for one item.

Place value. The idea that what a digit is worth depends on its position (its column) in the number. Example: In four thousand and eighty-two the eight is in the tens column, so it is worth eighty, and the four is in the thousands column, so it is worth four thousand. Watch out: A zero holds a column open: four thousand and eighty-two is not four hundred and eighty-two. Columns to the right of the decimal point get ten times smaller each step: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. Flip it: Reading a number (digits to values) and writing one from words (values to digits). The picture shows: Place value: each column is worth ten times the one on its right

Plan. The view of a three D shape from directly above, drawn flat. Examples: The plan of a cylinder standing on its end is a circle. The plan of a cuboid five centimetres by three centimetres by two centimetres, lying flat, is a five centimetres by three centimetres rectangle. Flip it: Working out the solid from its plan and elevations.

Polygon. A closed flat shape with straight sides. A shape with n sides has interior angles that add up to (n minus two) times one hundred and eighty degrees. Example: Triangle (three sides), quadrilateral (four), pentagon (five), hexagon (six), octagon (eight). Interior angles of a pentagon add to five hundred and forty degrees. Watch out: The exterior angles of a polygon add up to three hundred and sixty degrees. Flip it: From the number of sides to the angle total, or from an angle back to the number of sides. The picture shows: A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides

Position-to-term rule. Another name for the nth term: a formula that gives a term of a sequence from its position n. Example: For five, eight, eleven, fourteen, the position-to-term rule is three n plus two. Put n equals ten to get the 10th term, thirty-two. Flip it: From the rule to a term: put in n. From the terms to the rule: use the common difference.

Power (index). A small raised number that says how many times to multiply a number by itself. The plural of index is indices. Example: two to the power of five equals two times two times two times two times two equals thirty-two. Here two is the base and five is the power. Watch out: two to the power of five is not two times five. Flip it: Roots undo powers.

Pressure. How hard a force pushes on each unit of area. Pressure equals force divided by area. Examples: six hundred N on two metres squared is a pressure of three hundred N/m squared. The same force on a smaller area gives a bigger pressure. Watch out: A bigger area spreads the force out, so the pressure goes down. Flip it: From force and area to pressure, and from pressure and area to force.

Prime factorisation. Writing a number as a product of prime numbers. Every whole number bigger than one has exactly one prime factorisation (ignoring order). Example: eighty-four equals two times two times three times seven equals two squared times three times seven. A factor tree breaks a number into primes step by step. Watch out: Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime. one is not prime, so a branch never ends in one. Flip it: Break a number into primes, or multiply the primes together to rebuild it.

Prime number. A whole number with exactly two factors: one and itself. Example: Primes: two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, nine is not prime because three times three equals nine. Watch out: one is not prime (it has only one factor). two is the only even prime.

Prism. A solid with the same cross-section all the way along its length. Examples: Volume of a prism equals area of cross-section times length. A triangular prism with a cross-section that is a triangle of area ten centimetres squared, and a length of eight centimetres, has volume eighty centimetres cubed.

Probability. A number from zero to one that says how likely something is. zero means impossible and one means certain. Example: A fair coin lands heads with probability the fraction one over two,. A fair dice shows a six with probability the fraction one over six,. Watch out: Probabilities of all possible outcomes add up to one. Flip it: The probability of an event happening and the probability of it not happening add up to one. So the probability of not event equals one minus the probability of event.

Product. The result of multiplying numbers together. Example: The product of six and four is twenty-four. Watch out: In a shop a product is something you buy. In maths it is the answer to a multiplication. Flip it: Dividing the product by one of the numbers gives back the other: twenty-four divided by six equals four.

Profit. The money left after you take the costs away from the money you receive. Example: You buy a bike for eighty pounds and sell it for one hundred pounds. Profit equals one hundred minus eighty equals twenty pounds. Flip it: If the costs are more than the money received, the difference is a loss.

Proof. A chain of reasons that shows a statement is true in every case, not only in the examples you tried. Example: Examples show that the sides three, four, five and the sides five, twelve, thirteen fit eigh squared plus b squared equals c squared. A proof shows it works for every right-angled triangle. Watch out: A few examples are evidence, not proof.

Proportion. Two quantities are in proportion if one is always the same multiple of the other. When one doubles, so does the other. Example: If three pens cost two pounds forty, then six pens cost four pounds eighty. Flip it: Direct proportion (both rise together) and inverse proportion (one rises as the other falls).

Prove. A question word: show, with a chain of clear steps, that something is always true. One example is not enough. Example: Prove that the sum of two odd numbers is even. Write: odd numbers are two metres plus one and two n plus one. Their sum is two metres plus two n plus two equals two(m plus n plus one), which is a multiple of two, so it is even. Watch out: Trying a few numbers is not a proof. Use letters so the argument works for every number.

Pythagoras' theorem. In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: eigh squared plus b squared equals c squared, where c is the hypotenuse. Example: The two shorter sides are three and four: c squared equals nine plus sixteen equals twenty-five, so c equals five. Watch out: It works for right-angled triangles only. To find a short side, subtract: eigh squared equals c squared minus b squared. Flip it: Find the hypotenuse (add the squares) or find a shorter side (subtract). The converse tests whether a triangle is right-angled.

Pythagorean triple. Three whole numbers a, b and c that fit eigh squared plus b squared equals c squared. Example: three, four, five; five, twelve, thirteen; eight, fifteen, seventeen; seven, twenty-four, twenty-five. Doubling or tripling every number in a triple gives another triple, such as six, eight, ten.

Quadrant. One of the four regions the axes cut a grid into, numbered one to four anticlockwise from the top right. Example: minus three comma six is in quadrant two (top left), because x is negative and y is positive. Watch out: The numbering goes anticlockwise, not left to right.

Quadratic. An expression or equation where the highest power of the unknown is two. Example: x squared plus five x plus six equals zero is a quadratic equation. Its graph is a U-shaped curve called a parabola.

Quadratic formula. A formula that solves any equation ax squared plus bx plus c equals zero (where a is not zero): x equals (minus b ± square root of (b squared minus four ac)) divided by two eigh. Example: x squared minus six x plus two equals zero has eigh equals one, b equals minus six, c equals two. So x equals (six ± square root of twenty-eight) divided by two equals five point six five or zero point three five to two d.p. Watch out: If b is negative, then minus b is positive. Take care with the signs.

Quadratic inequality. An inequality that contains an x squared term, solved by sketching the graph of the quadratic and reading where it is above or below the x-axis. Examples: x squared minus x minus six is less than zero gives minus two is less than x is less than three. x squared minus x minus six is greater than zero gives x is less than minus two or x is greater than three. Watch out: For a U-shaped curve, below the axis is between the critical values and above the axis is outside them. Do not divide both sides by x.

Quadratic sequence. A sequence whose nth term contains n squared. The second differences (the gaps between the gaps) are constant. Example: four, nine, eighteen, thirty-one, has first differences five, nine, thirteen and second differences four, four. The nth term is two n squared minus n plus three.

Quartile. One of the three values that split data, in order from smallest to largest, into four equal parts: the lower quartile, the median and the upper quartile. Example: For eighty values, read the lower quartile at height twenty on a cumulative frequency graph, the median at forty and the upper quartile at sixty. Watch out: The height on the vertical axis tells you where to read. The quartile is the value on the horizontal axis. Flip it: If the upper quartile of eighty values is thirty-seven, then sixty of the values are thirty-seven or less.

Quotient. The result of dividing one number by another. Example: The quotient of twenty-four and six is four. When ninety-five is divided by four the quotient is twenty-three (with remainder three). Flip it: Multiplying the quotient by the divisor (and adding the remainder) gives back the number you started with.

Radius. The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge. The plural is radii. Example: The circle x squared plus y squared equals twenty-five has centre zero comma zero and radius five. The picture shows: The radius goes from the centre to the edge

Raffle. A prize draw. Every ticket sold has an equal chance of winning, so the more tickets you hold, the better your chance. Example: two hundred tickets are sold and you buy five. If there is one prize, the probability that you win is the fraction five over two hundred, equals the fraction one over forty,.

Range. A measure of spread: the biggest value minus the smallest. Example: two, three, seven, eight, twenty: range equals twenty minus two equals eighteen. Watch out: The range is a single number, not "two to twenty".

Ratio. A way of comparing quantities. A ratio tells you the shares, not the actual numbers. Example: A ratio of boys to girls of three: five means for every three boys there are five girls. If one part is x, there are three x boys and five x girls. Watch out: Order matters: boys to girls (three: five) is not girls to boys. Flip it: Sharing a total in a ratio, and finding the total (or a share) from one known amount.

Rational number. A number that can be written as a fraction with a whole number as the numerator and a whole number as the denominator. Its decimal either stops or repeats. Examples: zero point seven five equals the fraction three over four,, five equals the fraction five over one, and zero point three three three, equals the fraction one over three, are all rational. square root of sixteen equals four is rational. square root of two is not. Watch out: Every whole number is rational. A root is only irrational (a surd) when the number under it is not a perfect square. Flip it: A rational number is one that is not irrational.

Rationalising the denominator. Rewriting a fraction so there is no surd in the denominator. Multiply the numerator and denominator by a suitable surd. Example: the fraction one over square root of two, equals the fraction square root of two over two,. When the denominator is three minus square root of three, multiply the numerator and denominator by three plus square root of three: (three minus square root of three)(three plus square root of three) equals nine minus three equals six.

Reciprocal. The number you multiply a number by to get one. For a fraction, turn it upside down. Example: The reciprocal of the fraction three over four, is the fraction four over three,. The reciprocal of five is the fraction one over five,. the fraction three over four, times the fraction four over three, equals one. Watch out: Zero has no reciprocal, because nothing multiplied by zero gives one. Flip it: Dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.

Reflection. A transformation that flips a shape over a mirror line. Each point and its image are the same distance from the line, on opposite sides. Examples: Reflect the point one comma two in the line x equals three: the point is two left of the line, so the image is two right, at five comma two. In the line y equals x, the coordinates swap: one comma two goes to two comma one. Watch out: A point on the mirror line stays where it is. Flip it: From a shape and its image, the mirror line is halfway between matching points. The picture shows: A grid showing the point one comma two reflected in the line x equals three to five comma two, and in the line y equals x to two comma one

Reflex angle. An angle that is more than one hundred and eighty degrees and less than three hundred and sixty degrees. Example: two hundred and seventy degrees is reflex. A reflex angle and the angle on the other side of the same point together make three hundred and sixty degrees. The picture shows: A reflex angle, more than one hundred and eighty degrees

Regular polygon. A polygon where all the sides are equal and all the angles are equal. Example: A square and an equilateral triangle are regular. Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is one hundred and twenty degrees. Watch out: A shape can have equal sides without equal angles (a rhombus), and then it is not regular. Flip it: Each exterior angle is three hundred and sixty degrees divided by n, so n equals three hundred and sixty degrees divided by exterior angle. The picture shows: A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles

Relative frequency. An estimate of a probability from an experiment: the number of times something happened divided by the number of trials. Example: A dropped drawing pin lands point up eighteen times in fifty drops. Relative frequency equals eighteen divided by fifty equals zero point three six. Watch out: More trials give a better estimate. A few trials can be very misleading. Flip it: If you know the probability, expected number equals probability times number of trials.

Remainder. What is left over when one whole number does not divide exactly into another. Example: ninety-five divided by four equals twenty-three remainder three, because four times twenty-three equals ninety-two and ninety-five minus ninety-two equals three. Watch out: In a real problem, a remainder often means you need one more: seventy students in sixteen-seat minibuses need five minibuses, not four. Flip it: The original number equals divisor times quotient plus remainder.

Reverse percentage. Working backwards from the value after a percentage change to find the original value. Example: After a twenty percent discount a coat costs forty-eight pounds. The multiplier is zero point eight, so the original price equals forty-eight divided by zero point eight equals sixty pounds. Watch out: Do not add twenty percent back onto forty-eight pounds. The twenty percent was taken from the original, not from forty-eight pounds.

Right angle. An angle of exactly ninety degrees, like the corner of a page. It is marked with a small square. Example: The corner of a rectangle. The picture shows: A right angle, exactly ninety degrees

Root (solution) of an equation. A value of the unknown that makes the equation true. A quadratic can have two roots. On its graph, the roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis. Example: x squared minus x minus six equals zero has roots x equals three and x equals minus two. Flip it: Roots two and five come from the brackets (x minus two)(x minus five).

Rotation. A transformation that turns a shape about a fixed point called the centre. To describe it you give the angle, the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise) and the centre. Examples: Rotate the point two comma one by ninety degrees clockwise about the origin: x comma y goes to (y, minus x), giving one comma minus two. A half turn about the origin: x comma y goes to (minus x, minus y). Watch out: A ninety degrees turn clockwise is the same as two hundred and seventy degrees anticlockwise.

Rotational symmetry. A shape has rotational symmetry if it fits onto itself after being turned by less than a full turn about its centre. The order is the number of ways it fits in one full turn. Examples: A square has rotational symmetry of order four. The smallest turn that fits is three hundred and sixty degrees divided by four equals ninety degrees. A shape with order one has no rotational symmetry.

Round (rounding). Replace a number with a nearby simpler one to a stated accuracy, such as the nearest ten, a number of decimal places or a number of significant figures. Example: three thousand, four hundred and sixty-eight to the nearest one hundred is three thousand, five hundred. six point seven four nine to one decimal place is six point seven. Watch out: Look only at the digit just after the place you are rounding to: five or more rounds up, four or less rounds down. Flip it: Rounding finds the nearest simple number; going backwards asks which numbers round to a given one (the whole numbers thirty-five to forty-four all round to forty to the nearest ten).

Salary. Money paid for a job as a fixed amount for the year, usually paid in equal monthly parts. Example: A salary of twenty-four thousand pounds a year is twenty-four thousand pounds divided by twelve equals two thousand pounds a month.

Sample space. The list or table of every possible outcome. A sample-space diagram is a table that shows them all, so none are missed. Example: For two dice, the sample space has thirty-six pairs of scores, from one comma one to six comma six. Flip it: Count the pairs you want in the table and divide by the total number of pairs to get a probability.

Scalar. An ordinary number, used to multiply a vector. Multiplying a vector by a scalar makes it longer or shorter, and a negative scalar reverses its direction. Examples: three times the vector two comma minus one is six comma minus three. minus one times a vector gives the opposite vector. Watch out: Vectors that are scalar multiples of each other are parallel.

Scale drawing. A drawing that is similar to the real thing, with every length reduced (or enlarged) by the same scale factor. Examples: On a scale of one: fifty, a wall that is eight centimetres long on the plan is four hundred centimetres (four metres) in real life. Flip it: Real length to drawing length (divide), and drawing length to real length (multiply).

Scale factor. The number all lengths are multiplied by in an enlargement. If lengths are multiplied by k, areas are multiplied by k squared and volumes by k cubed. Example: Scale factor three: a two centimetres line becomes six centimetres, a four centimetres squared area becomes thirty-six centimetres squared.

Scatter graph. A graph of points, each showing two measurements for one person or thing, used to see whether the two are linked. Example: Plot hours of revision against test score for each student. Watch out: A link on a scatter graph does not prove that one thing causes the other. Flip it: Draw a line of best fit, then use it to estimate one value from the other.

Sector. A slice of a circle between two radii and the arc that joins their ends. Examples: A sector with angle seventy-two degrees and radius five centimetres is the fraction seventy-two over three hundred and sixty, equals the fraction one over five, of the circle. Its area is ⅕ times pi times five squared equals fifteen point seven centimetres squared (to one d.p.). Watch out: Find the fraction of the circle first: angle divided by three hundred and sixty degrees.

Segment (of a circle). The region of a circle between a chord and the arc it cuts off. A chord splits a circle into a small segment and a big segment. Examples: The shaded piece of a circle cut off by a straight line across it is a segment. If the chord is a diameter, each segment is a semicircle. Watch out: A sector is a slice between two radii. A segment is cut off by a chord.

Semicircle. Half of a circle, cut along a diameter. Examples: A semicircle with diameter eight centimetres has radius four centimetres, so its area is ½ times pi times four squared equals twenty-five point one centimetres squared. Its perimeter is the curved edge plus the straight eight centimetres. Watch out: The perimeter of a semicircle includes the straight edge, not only the curve.
Sequence. A list of numbers that follow a rule. Each number is a term of the sequence. Example: three, seven, eleven, fifteen, goes up by four each time.

Show that. A question word: the answer is given to you, and you must prove it is right by writing every step. The marks are for the working. Example: Show that x equals four is a solution of three x minus one equals eleven. Write three times four minus one equals eleven. Watch out: Do not write only the answer: it is already in the question.

Significant figure (s.f.). The digits of a number that matter, counting from the first digit that is not zero. "To two s.f." keeps the first two of them. Example: four thousand, three hundred and seventy-two to two s.f. is four thousand, four hundred. zero point zero zero three eight hundred and sixty-two to two s.f. is zero point zero zero three nine. Watch out: Zeros at the start do not count. Zeros that hold the place value at the end are still needed (four thousand, four hundred, not forty-four).

Similar shapes. Shapes that are enlargements of each other: the same shape, different size. All the angles match and all the lengths are in the same ratio. Example: Any two squares are similar. A square and a two by one rectangle are not. Watch out: In everyday English "similar" means "a bit alike". In maths it is exact: same shape, scaled.

Simple interest. Interest worked out only on the starting amount, so the same amount is paid every year. Example: six hundred pounds at three percent simple interest for four years. three percent of six hundred pounds equals eighteen pounds a year, so the interest is four times eighteen equals seventy-two pounds. Watch out: Simple interest does not earn interest on the interest. Compound interest does. Flip it: Find the rate or the time from the interest paid: rate equals interest divided by (amount times years).

Simplify. Make an expression shorter or neater without changing its value, for example by collecting like terms. Examples: five x plus two minus x plus four simplifies to four x plus six eigh times a simplifies to eigh squared Watch out: For fractions, simplifying means writing them in lowest terms (see Simplify a fraction).

Simplify a fraction. Write a fraction in its lowest terms: divide the numerator and denominator by the same number until no number except one divides both. Example: the fraction twelve over eighteen,: divide the numerator and denominator by six to get the fraction two over three,. the fraction two over three, cannot be simplified further. Watch out: Examiners expect the simplest form unless the question says otherwise. Divide by the HCF to finish in one step. Flip it: Simplifying is the reverse of making an equivalent fraction.

Simultaneous equations. Two or more equations that are all true at the same time for the same values of the unknowns. For two straight-line equations, the solution is where their graphs cross. Example: x plus y equals five and x minus y equals one are both true when x equals three and y equals two.

Sine (sin). For an angle in a right-angled triangle, sine is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse. Examples: If the opposite side is three and the hypotenuse is five, sin x equals the fraction three over five,. sin thirty degrees equals zero point five. Watch out: Make sure your calculator is in degrees. In a right-angled triangle, sine is never more than one. Flip it: Finding a side with sin, and finding the angle with sin to the power of minus one.

Sine rule. For any triangle: a / sin eigh equals b / sin B equals c / sin C, where side a is opposite angle eigh, and so on. Use it when you know a side and the angle opposite it, and one more side or angle. Example: Side eigh equals six is opposite angle eigh equals thirty degrees. Find side b, which is opposite angle B equals forty-five degrees. Watch out: When finding an angle, there may be two answers (see ambiguous case).

Sketch. A question word: draw a quick, rough picture that shows the main features. It does not need to be exact, but it must have the right shape and label the key points. Example: Sketch the graph of y equals x squared minus four. Draw a U-shaped curve that crosses the x-axis at minus two and two, and the y-axis at minus four. Watch out: Sketch is not the same as draw. Draw means accurate, with a ruler and compasses. Sketch means rough. Label the points the question asks for.

soh cah toa. A memory aid for the three trig ratios: Sin equals Opposite divided by Hypotenuse, Cos equals Adjacent divided by Hypotenuse, Tan equals Opposite divided by Adjacent. Example: You know the adjacent side and want the hypotenuse. Adjacent and Hypotenuse are the eigh and H in CAH, so use cos. Flip it: Choosing the ratio from the sides, and naming the sides from the ratio.

Solve. Find the value (or values) of the unknown that make an equation true. Example: Solve three x plus five equals twenty: take five from both sides (three x equals fifteen), then divide both by three (x equals five). Watch out: Check your answer by putting it back into the equation. three times five plus five equals twenty ✓

Speed. How far something travels in each unit of time. Speed equals distance divided by time. Examples: one hundred and fifty kilometres in two point five hours is one hundred and fifty divided by two point five equals sixty kilometres/h. Rearranged: distance equals speed times time, and time equals distance divided by speed. Watch out: For km/h the time must be in hours. one hour thirty minutes is one point five hours, not one point three. Flip it: From distance and time to speed, and from speed and time to distance.

Square number. The answer when a whole number is multiplied by itself. Example: one, four, nine, sixteen, twenty-five, thirty-six, (one squared, two squared, three squared, four squared, ). seven squared equals seven times seven equals forty-nine. Flip it: Squaring and square-rooting undo each other: seven squared equals forty-nine and square root of forty-nine equals seven. The picture shows: A square number is the area of a square: three times three is nine

Square root. The positive number that, multiplied by itself, gives the number you started with. Written with the sign square root of. Example: square root of eighty-one equals nine because nine times nine equals eighty-one. Watch out: Every positive number has two square roots (nine and minus nine both square to eighty-one). The square root of sign means the positive one; solving x squared equals eighty-one gives x equals nine or x equals minus nine. Flip it: The inverse of squaring, for numbers that are zero or more.

Standard form. A way to write very big or very small numbers as a number from one up to (but not including) ten, times a power of ten. Examples: four million, five hundred thousand equals four point five times ten to the power of six zero point zero zero zero seven two equals seven point two times ten to the power of minus four Watch out: forty-five times ten cubed is not in standard form, because forty-five is not less than ten. Flip it: Move the decimal point the other way to change standard form back into an ordinary number.

Subject (of a formula). The letter on its own on one side of a formula, usually the left. Making a letter the subject means rearranging the formula so that letter is alone. Examples: In v equals u plus at, the subject is v. Make t the subject: subtract u from both sides, then divide by a, to get t equals the fraction v minus u over eigh,. Watch out: Use the same step on both sides, and divide the whole of the other side, not only one term. Flip it: Substituting puts numbers in to find the output. Making a letter the subject builds the formula that finds an input.

Substitute. Replace a letter with a number, then work out the answer. Example: Substitute x equals four into three x minus one: three times four minus one equals eleven. Flip it: Substituting goes from a letter to a value. Solving goes from a value back to the letter.

Sum. The result of adding numbers together. Example: The sum of seven and five is twelve. Watch out: In everyday English "a sum" can mean any calculation. In maths it is specifically the answer to an addition. Flip it: Subtraction undoes a sum: if the sum of seven and five is twelve, then twelve minus five equals seven.

Surd. A root that cannot be written as a whole number or a fraction. A surd is an exact answer, so keep it as a root. Example: square root of two and three square root of five are surds. square root of sixteen is not (it is four). square root of eighteen equals three square root of two. Watch out: A calculator shows a rounded decimal. If a question says "exact", leave the surd in.

Surface area. The total area of all the faces of a solid. Examples: A cuboid five centimetres by four centimetres by two centimetres has three pairs of matching faces, with areas twenty centimetres squared, ten centimetres squared and eight centimetres squared. Surface area equals two times (twenty plus ten plus eight) equals seventy-six centimetres squared. Watch out: Surface area is measured in square units, even though the solid is three D.

Tan (the trig ratio). For an angle in a right-angled triangle, tan is the opposite side divided by the adjacent side. It is not the same as a tangent line to a circle. Examples: If the opposite side is three and the adjacent side is four, tan x equals the fraction three over four,. tan forty-five degrees equals one. Watch out: Tan can be bigger than one. It does not use the hypotenuse. Flip it: Finding a side with tan, and finding the angle with tan to the power of minus one.

Tangent. A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point. It is perpendicular to the radius at that point. Example: A bike wheel resting on flat ground: the ground is a tangent to the wheel. The picture shows: A tangent touches the circle at one point

Term. One part of an expression. Terms are separated by plus and minus signs, and each term keeps the sign in front of it. Example: four x minus seven y plus three has three terms: four x, minus seven y and three. Watch out: This is different from "term" in sequences (the terms of a sequence are its numbers).

Term-to-term rule. A rule that tells you how to get from one term of a sequence to the next. Example: three, seven, eleven, fifteen, has the term-to-term rule "add four". Watch out: It is slow for a term far along the sequence. The nth term jumps straight there. Flip it: From the terms to the rule: find the gap between neighbouring terms.

Tessellation. A pattern of the same tile repeated to cover a flat surface, with no gaps and no overlaps. Examples: Squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons tessellate on their own. A brick wall is a tessellation of rectangles.

Tip (gratuity). A small extra amount of money given to thank someone for a service, often a percentage of the bill. Example: A ten percent tip on a thirty pounds meal is zero point one times thirty equals three pounds. Watch out: The tip is on top of the bill, so the total is bill plus tip.

Tolerance. How far a measurement is allowed to be from its target. A tolerance of two millimetres on a six hundred millimetre length means five hundred and ninety-eight millimetres to six hundred and two millimetres. Examples: A pipe cut to two point five zero metres with a tolerance of five millimetres either way is between two thousand, four hundred and ninety-five millimetres and two thousand, five hundred and five millimetres.

Transformation. A rule that moves a shape or changes its size. The four you need are translation, reflection, rotation and enlargement. Examples: Slide a triangle three squares right: a translation. Flip the triangle over a line: a reflection. Flip it: From a shape and its image, describe the single transformation that links them.

Translation. A transformation that slides every point the same distance in the same direction. The shape does not turn, flip or change size. Examples: Translate the point two comma three by the column vector with four on top and one underneath: add four to x and one to y, giving six comma four. Watch out: The top number of the vector is the move across (negative is left). The bottom number is the move up (negative is down). Flip it: From a shape and its image, find the vector: image point minus object point.

Trapezium. A four-sided shape with one pair of parallel sides. The plural is trapezia. Examples: The parallel sides are six centimetres and ten centimetres, and the perpendicular height between them is four centimetres. Area equals ½ times (six plus ten) times four equals thirty-two centimetres squared. Watch out: Add the two parallel sides, then halve. The slanting sides are not used in the area.

Tree diagram. A diagram of branches showing all possible outcomes of two or more events, with probabilities on the branches. Multiply the probabilities along the branches, and add the probabilities of the end results you want. Example: Two flips of a fair coin: the probability of head then head equals the fraction one over two, times the fraction one over two, equals the fraction one over four,.

Truncation. Cutting off the digits after a chosen place without rounding. Examples: seven point three eight truncated to one decimal place is seven point three (rounding would give seven point four). If a number is four point six after truncation to one d.p., then four point six is less than or equal to x is less than four point seven. Watch out: The original number is at least the truncated value and less than one rounding unit above it, so the error interval is not half a unit each way.

Turning point. The point where a graph changes direction: a minimum if it goes down then up, a maximum if it goes up then down. Example: For y equals (x minus p) squared plus q the turning point is p comma q.

Two-way table. A table that sorts the same people or things in two ways at once, with rows for one grouping, columns for the other and totals at the ends. Example: Boys and girls (rows) against walk and bus (columns). The eighteen in the girls row and the walk column means that eighteen girls walk. Watch out: Check that the rows, columns and totals add up before you use the numbers. Flip it: Fill in the totals first if they are missing, then work backwards to find the missing cells.

Unitary method. Find the value of one unit first, then multiply to get the amount you want. Example: five tiles cost twelve pounds fifty, so one tile costs two pounds fifty and eight tiles cost eight times two pounds fifty equals twenty pounds. Flip it: Dividing to find one, then multiplying to find many.

Unknown (variable). A letter standing for a number. It is called an unknown when you are trying to find it, and a variable when it can take many values. Example: In three x plus two equals fourteen the unknown is x (and x equals four).

Upper bound. The limit at the top of the possible values of a rounded or measured number. For a rounded number it is the number plus half the rounding unit. Examples: A plank of length two point four metres, to one decimal place, has upper bound two point four plus zero point zero five equals two point four five metres. seven to the nearest whole number has upper bound seven point five. Watch out: Values just below the upper bound still round to the number, but the upper bound itself would round up, so an error interval uses is less than at this end.

VAT. Value added tax: a percentage added to the price of most goods and services. The usual UK rate is twenty percent. Example: A bike costs two hundred and fifty pounds before VAT. With twenty percent VAT: two hundred and fifty times one point two equals three hundred pounds. Watch out: To take VAT out of a price that includes it, divide by one point two. Taking twenty percent off the price does not work. Flip it: Price without VAT equals price with VAT divided by one point two.

Vector. A journey with a size and a direction, such as three right and two up. It is drawn as an arrow and written as a column vector, or as a bold letter such as a. Examples: The vector from eigh one comma two to B five comma five is B minus eigh equals four comma three. Equal vectors have the same length and direction, wherever they are drawn. Watch out: AB is end minus start. BA is the opposite vector: BA equals minus AB. Flip it: From two points, write the vector. From a vector and one point, find the other point.

Venn diagram. A diagram of overlapping circles in a box. Each circle is a set, the overlap holds what is in both sets, and the space outside the circles holds what is in neither. Example: In a class of thirty students, eighteen like football, twelve like rugby and five like both. So thirteen like football only, five like both, seven like rugby only and five like neither. Watch out: Fill in the overlap first. Items in both sets must not be counted twice. Flip it: From the numbers in each region you can read off probabilities, such as the probability of neither equals the fraction five over thirty,.

Vertically opposite angles. The angles that face each other when two straight lines cross (an X shape). They are always equal. Example: If one angle is forty-eight degrees, the angle directly opposite is also forty-eight degrees, and each of the other two is one hundred and thirty-two degrees. Watch out: Angles next to each other on a straight line are not vertically opposite: they add to one hundred and eighty degrees. The picture shows: Vertically opposite angles are equal

Volume. The amount of space inside a solid. It is measured in cubic units such as cm cubed and m cubed. Examples: A cuboid six centimetres by four centimetres by three centimetres has volume six times four times three equals seventy-two centimetres cubed. Watch out: one metre cubed equals one million centimetres cubed and one thousand centimetres cubed equals one litre. Flip it: From volume to a missing length: divide the volume by the other measurements.

Wage. Money paid for work, usually worked out per hour or per week. Example: A wage of twelve pounds an hour for seven hours is twelve times seven equals eighty-four pounds. Watch out: A salary is similar, but it is a fixed amount for the year, usually paid monthly.

Without replacement. When an item is taken and not put back, so the second pick has one fewer to choose from and the probabilities change. Example: A bag with three red and two blue counters. The probability that the first pick is red is the fraction three over five,. The probability that the second pick is also red, with no replacement, is the fraction two over four,.

Work out. A question word: find the answer by doing the calculation. Show your steps when there are marks for working. Example: Work out three plus four times two. Answer: four times two equals eight, then three plus eight equals eleven. Watch out: Calculate means almost the same. Write down means no working is needed.

Work shift. The fixed block of hours a person works in one go, for example nine am to five pm. Example: A shift from nine:thirty am to five:fifteen pm is seven hours forty-five minutes long. Watch out: Count from the start time to the end time. Take off any unpaid break if the question says so.
Write down. A question word: give the answer only. No working is needed. Example: Write down the next number in two, four, six, eight. Answer: ten.

y-intercept. The value of y where a line crosses the y-axis (where x equals zero). In y equals mx plus c it is c. Example: The line y equals three x minus two crosses the y-axis at zero comma minus two, so its y-intercept is minus two. Watch out: It is where the line meets the y-axis, not the x-axis. Flip it: To find where a line crosses the x-axis, put y equals zero instead.

Units and money Give the unit in your answer: twelve minutes, forty-five metres, three centimetres. When you read a value off a graph, give your answer to the nearest whole number. Answers a little either side are accepted, because nobody can read a curve exactly. Round money to two decimal places. If the question says one decimal place, do that.
